api/DBTools.Core.Revit.Execution.CallGat.summary: Interface IRevitCallGate Namespace DBTools.Core.Revit.Execution.CallGate Assembly DBTools.Core.dll Unified entry point for executing Revit API callbacks either inline (modal) or queued (modeless). public interface IRevitCallGate Remarks Null work delegates and rejected delegate shapes throw from the call itself. Failures after argument validation, including cancellation, mode or context refusal, callback failure, and erased awaitable-result rejection, are delivered through the returned task. Cancellation completes the task as Canceled. An OperationCanceledException thrown by a gate check or work delegate is rethrown; cancellation observed by the queued host surfaces as a TaskCanceledException. Properties InGate True when currently executing within a call-gate callback on the Revit UI thread. bool InGate { get; } Property Value bool Methods RunAsync(Action<UIApplication>, CancellationToken, RevitCallGateMode) Executes the work delegate on the Revit UI thread. Null work and async-state-machine Action delegates throw from the call before execution. Task RunAsync(Action<UIApplication> work, CancellationToken ct = default, RevitCallGateMode mode = RevitCallGateMode.Auto) Parameters work Action<UIApplication> ct CancellationToken mode RevitCallGateMode Returns Task Remarks Queued work that has not started when the owning call-gate task retires is dropped, and its task never completes, even if its cancellation token is cancelled later. Callers must not await or block on such a task during shutdown. Failed-startup cleanup cancels pending work instead. RunAsync<T>(Func<UIApplication, T>, CancellationToken, RevitCallGateMode) Executes the work delegate on the Revit UI thread and returns a result. Task and ValueTask result shapes and reference-typed multicast result delegates throw from the call before execution. An erased Task or boxed ValueTask result (for example, a Task returned as object or an interface) is rejected only after the work runs. Its side effects remain, and any started Task continues running. Other awaitable types (for example, ConfigureAwait results and custom awaiters) are not detected. api/DBTools.Core.Revit.Execution.CallGat.summary: Class RevitCallGateTask Namespace DBTools.Core.Revit.Execution.CallGate Assembly DBTools.Core.dll Owns one ExternalEvent and its FIFO work queue for one add-in lifetime. public sealed class RevitCallGateTask : IRevitCallGateTask, IExternalEventHandler, IDisposable, IAsyncDisposable Inheritance object RevitCallGateTask Implements IRevitCallGateTask IExternalEventHandler IDisposable IAsyncDisposable Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Each native Execute runs the work that was queued when it started, in order, until the DBTools.Core.Revit.Execution.CallGate.RevitCallGateTask.DrainBudget is used. Work queued during the turn, or left by the budget, waits for the next raise, which is posted to the dispatcher and so runs after Execute returns. Revit discards what a callback leaves open only when the callback returns. A call ends the turn when it leaves a transaction open in any document, or when it creates a transaction group, which every production group owner reports through DBTools.Core.Revit.Execution.CallGate.RevitCallGateTurnBoundary. No later call of the turn then runs inside state that an earlier call left open. Every raise is posted, also from the dispatcher thread, so a caller never waits on native Raise. Turn timing is logged at Debug level, throttled by DBTools.Core.Revit.Execution.CallGate.RevitCallGateTurnStatistics. Retirement drops queued delegates and registrations without completing their tasks. Such tasks never finish: a worker synchronously waiting on one would remain blocked. Callers must use asynchronous lifetimes and must not wait for retired work during shutdown. Failed-startup cleanup uses CancelPending instead, so callers in the live process observe cancellation. api/DBTools.Core.Revit.Transactions.Tran.summary: Class TransactionFailurePreprocessor Namespace DBTools.Core.Revit.Transactions Assembly DBTools.Core.dll Preprocessor that suppresses Revit warnings and prevents Revit's failure UI from surfacing. Warnings are deleted. Errors/fatal failures cause the transaction to roll back (no Revit dialogs) so DBTools can surface the error. public sealed class TransactionFailurePreprocessor : IFailuresPreprocessor Inheritance object TransactionFailurePreprocessor Implements IFailuresPreprocessor Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Properties AccessorFaults public List<Exception> AccessorFaults { get; } Property Value List<Exception> BlockingFailureCount public int BlockingFailureCount { get; } Property Value int BlockingFailureDefinitionIds public List<FailureDefinitionId> BlockingFailureDefinitionIds { get; } Property Value List<FailureDefinitionId> BlockingFailureMessages public List<string> BlockingFailureMessages { get; } Property Value List<string> FailureRecords Every failure message read during commit, with its definition, failing elements and resolution. public List<TransactionFailureRecord> FailureRecords { get; } Property Value List<TransactionFailureRecord> LastResult public FailureProcessingResult LastResult { get; } Property Value FailureProcessingResult SuppressedWarningCount public int SuppressedWarningCount { get; } Property Value int SuppressedWarningMessages public List<string> SuppressedWarningMessages { get; } Property Value List<string> Methods AttachToTransaction(Transaction) Attach a silent warning preprocessor to an active transaction. public static TransactionFailurePreprocessor AttachToTransaction(Transaction tx) Parameters tx Transaction Returns TransactionFailurePreprocessor PreprocessFailures(FailuresAccessor) This method is called when there have been failures found at the end of a transaction and Revit is about to start processing them. public FailureProcessingResult PreprocessFailures(FailuresAccessor a) Parameters a FailuresAccessor Returns FailureProcessingResult Notifies end of transaction code about further actions required. Return values are interpreted as follows: Continue - the failure processing will continue. Failures will be shown to the user, even if they were addressed by this method. ProceedWithCommit - end of transaction checks and failure processing will restart from the beginning. If some failures were resolved here, they will be removed and not delivered to the user. ProceedWithCommit cannot be returned if transaction is being rolled back. ProceedWithRollBack - the failure processing will continue. Failures will be shown to the user, but user will have no option to resolve or ignore them - only cancel option will be available. If intent is to roll back transaction without showing failures to the user, it can be achieved by setting failure handling option to remove failures before returning ProceedWithRollBack. Other return values are not allowed.

api/DBTools.Core.Revit.Transactions.Tran.summary: Interface IAtomicTransactionGroup Namespace DBTools.Core.Revit.Transactions.TransactionGroup Assembly DBTools.Core.dll Runs work inside one transaction group within a single Revit API callback, so the group becomes exactly one Revit Undo entry. Revit rolls back a group that is still open when the callback that started it returns, so a group must never span call-gate calls. public interface IAtomicTransactionGroup Methods RunAsync<T>(string, Func<CancellationToken, Task<T>>, Func<T, bool>, CancellationToken) Begins the group on the active document, runs work, then assimilates the group when keep accepts the result and rolls it back otherwise. An exception, or cancellation seen at any point before finalization, rolls the group back and propagates. The work must complete within the callback: its call-gate calls run inline. A document with an open transaction is refused before any work. Unless Revit confirms the rollback, the call throws TransactionGroupOutcomeUnknownException. api/DBTools.Core.Settings.Persistence.IS.summary: Interface ISettingsProvider Namespace DBTools.Core.Settings.Persistence Assembly DBTools.Core.dll Reads layered settings and atomically commits per-year sections. public interface ISettingsProvider Methods CommitAsync(IReadOnlyCollection<SettingsSectionWrite>, CancellationToken) Replaces the supplied per-year sections with one atomic file swap. Task CommitAsync(IReadOnlyCollection<SettingsSectionWrite> writes, CancellationToken ct = default) Parameters writes IReadOnlyCollection<SettingsSectionWrite> ct CancellationToken Returns Task Remarks Rejects an empty batch, null entries and repeated sections. Acquires a cross-process lock and rereads the file before replacing sections. Lock acquisition throws IOException after 10 seconds. A failed commit leaves the settings file unchanged. Get<TSettings>(SettingsSection<TSettings>) Synchronously rereads defaults and per-year settings without caching. TSettings Get<TSettings>(SettingsSection<TSettings> section) where TSettings : class, new() Parameters section SettingsSection<TSettings> Returns TSettings Type Parameters TSettings Remarks Missing files, sections and optional values use defaults. A value of the wrong JSON kind at an object or collection position reads as empty. An object, array or null at a string property reads as an empty string. A later file's null or scalar preserves an earlier object or array. Malformed JSON and missing JsonRequired members throw, including members of objects that read as empty. Values that cannot convert to a boolean or number throw, including null, objects and arrays. Other I/O errors propagate.

api/DBTools.Core.Tools.Commands.ToolComm.summary: Class ToolCommand Namespace DBTools.Core.Tools.Commands Assembly DBTools.Core.dll Base class for Revit commands to enforce ISafeExecutor, run-scope creation, and centralized error notification. [SuppressMessage("Usage", "VSTHRD002:Avoid problematic synchronous waits", Justification = "Revit IExternalCommand.Execute() must be synchronous - async pattern is for internal composability")] public abstract class ToolCommand : IExternalCommand, IExternalCommandAvailability Inheritance object ToolCommand Implements IExternalCommand IExternalCommandAvailability Derived AnalyticalSnapToLevelCommand ErftNewCommand ElevationTagsCommand MoveCombinedFoundationTagsCommand UpdateCombinedFoundationTagsCommand AllowJoinSelectedCommand DisallowJoinSelectedCommand GmCommand UpdateJoistGirderWeightsCommand OrganizeFoundationTypesCommand RecordSetCommand SgtCommand SettingsCommand TdvExportCommand TdvImportCommand VtcCommand Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks The parameterless constructor stays inert to satisfy Revit's Autodesk.Revit.UI.IExternalCommand contract. Runtime services are resolved during Execute(ExternalCommandData, ref string, ElementSet). Sync-over-Async Pattern: The Execute(ExternalCommandData, ref string, ElementSet) method uses .GetAwaiter().GetResult() because Revit's Execute(ExternalCommandData, ref string, ElementSet) method must return synchronously. The async pattern in RunAsync(ICommandContext) is for composability within the command implementation. Constructors ToolCommand() Creates a command that defers runtime service resolution until execute time. This is required by Revit's IExternalCommand contract (parameterless constructor). protected ToolCommand() Properties RequiresActiveDocument Whether the command works on the active document. A command that changes only application state returns false: its context captures no document, so it also runs when no model is open. protected virtual bool RequiresActiveDocument { get; } Property Value bool Methods Execute(ExternalCommandData, ref string, ElementSet) Overload this method to implement and external command within Revit. public Result Execute(ExternalCommandData commandData, ref string message, ElementSet elements) Parameters commandData ExternalCommandData An ExternalCommandData object which contains reference to Application and View needed by external command. message string Error message can be returned by external command. This will be displayed only if the command status was "Failed". There is a limit of 1023 characters for this message; strings longer than this will be truncated. elements ElementSet Element set indicating problem elements to display in the failure dialog. This will be used only if the command status was "Failed". Returns Result The result indicates if the execution fails, succeeds, or was canceled by user. If it does not succeed, Revit will undo any changes made by the external command. IsCommandAvailable(UIApplication, CategorySet) Implement this method to provide control over whether your external command is enabled or disabled. public bool IsCommandAvailable(UIApplication applicationData, CategorySet selectedCategories) Parameters applicationData UIApplication An ApplicationServices.Application object which contains reference to Application needed by external command. selectedCategories CategorySet An list of categories of the elements which have been selected in Revit in the active document, or an empty set if no elements are selected or there is no active document. Returns bool Indicates whether Revit should enable or disable the corresponding external command. Remarks This callback will be called by Revit's user interface any time there is a contextual change. Therefore, the callback must be fast and is not permitted to modify the active document and be blocking in any way. IsCommandAvailableCore(UIApplication, CategorySet) Evaluates the command's Revit context predicate without resolving application runtime services. protected virtual bool IsCommandAvailableCore(UIApplication applicationData, CategorySet selectedCategories) Parameters applicationData UIApplication selectedCategories CategorySet Returns bool RunAsync(ICommandContext) protected abstract Task RunAsync(ICommandContext context) Parameters context ICommandContext Returns Task

When no dispatcher is available or it is shutting down, the call throws instead of returning a task. public static Task Post(Action action, DispatcherPriority priority = DispatcherPriority.Normal) Parameters action Action priority DispatcherPriority Returns Task Remarks A post made after the application generation retires its dispatcher operations is refused before it reaches the dispatcher, and its task is canceled. api/DBTools.Presentation.ToolWindows.ITo.title: Interface IToolWindowSession | DB Tools
api/DBTools.Presentation.ToolWindows.ITo.summary: Interface IToolWindowSession Namespace DBTools.Presentation.ToolWindows Assembly DBTools.Presentation.dll Owns a raw-XAML view and its stable window shell. public interface IToolWindowSession Remarks Register payload event handlers and cleanup through the session. Retire synchronously on the shell's UI thread before unloading a payload generation. Window and View are unavailable after retirement. ShowDialog returns null after retirement. Host-owned creation, lifecycle, root layout and dispatcher callbacks temporarily clear contextual reflection and restore the caller's scope on return. Raw templates resolve through the stable schema. The close gate, subscribed handlers and AddCleanup callbacks re-enter the creation context with ExecutionContext flow suppressed. Retirement releases that context on every exit. Flow suppression prevents captures. Clearing contextual reflection controls synchronous resolution. A command must suppress flow throughout its payload reflection scope, including tool-triggered layout outside shell overrides. WPF can measure an invalidated subtree directly. This work can see the command context but cannot capture it while flow is suppressed. Async callback continuations do not inherit that context. Name resolution after an await must explicitly re-enter it under suppression for synchronous work. Binding accessors, edit cancellation, collection notifications and custom shell initializers execute in the host's neutral reflection context. They must not depend on ambient name resolution. Properties Closed Completes after an accepted user close, once every AddCleanup callback has run. Task Closed { get; } Property Value Task Remarks Forced retirement leaves this task pending, and it never completes. Callers must not await or block on it during shutdown or reload. Register retirement-time work through AddCleanup, never through a continuation of this task. IsRetired bool IsRetired { get; } Property Value bool Outcome Open until retirement starts. Retire records Closed for an accepted user close or Retired for a forced retirement, including native window destruction, once and before any AddCleanup callback runs. ToolWindowOutcome Outcome { get; } Property Value ToolWindowOutcome View FrameworkElement View { get; } Property Value FrameworkElement Window Window Window { get; } Property Value Window Methods AddCleanup(Action) void AddCleanup(Action cleanup) Parameters cleanup Action Close(bool?, bool) void Close(bool? dialogResult = null, bool bypassGate = false) Parameters dialogResult bool? bypassGate bool HideForPick() void HideForPick() RequestClose() void RequestClose() Require<T>(string) T Require<T>(string name) where T : class Parameters name string Returns T Type Parameters T Retire() Synchronously retires the owned stable graph through the same path after either close kind. Writers are quiesced before behavior release, LIFO cleanup and edit cancellation. Final discovery and severing include disconnected containers and owned popup roots. UI Automation may retain the stable tree; its bindings, resources, inputs and values must no longer retain the payload. Shared stable definitions are not mutated. Forced retirement suppresses payload close notifications. Accepted user close preserves pending form edits and Explicit bindings through Closed and cleanup. Neither path pumps. Register payload event unsubscriptions and other owned work through AddCleanup. IReadOnlyList<Exception> Retire() Returns IReadOnlyList<Exception> Show() void Show() ShowDialog() Shows a modal window with contextual reflection cleared and ExecutionContext flow suppressed throughout WPF's nested loop. Returns null when forced retirement ends the loop; a normal close preserves its dialog result. bool? ShowDialog() Returns bool? api/index.html.title: API reference | DB Tools
api/index.html.summary: API reference This section is generated from the XML documentation comments in the source code. It lists the public types and members of the DBTools assemblies. Generating the reference Run the documentation build from the repository root: bash .github/scripts/build-docs.sh full-api Use the SDK pinned by global.json. The script restores DocFX 2.78.5 from wiki/.config/dotnet-tools.json. It builds the Release product and Sandbox for Revit 2026 to supply build tasks, dependency assemblies and generated WPF source. The build runs on Linux with Windows targeting enabled. It does not start Revit. The script restores each non-test project in src/ with the metadata properties from wiki/docfx.json. DocFX's automatic restore is disabled because version 2.78.5 does not pass these properties to dotnet restore: Property Value Purpose Configuration Release Match the prerequisite builds and DocFX's default configuration. RevitYear 2026 Select the Revit API packages and year-specific restore assets. EnableWindowsTargeting true Resolve Windows and WPF reference packs on Linux. Set for every project by Directory.Build.props. DesignTimeBuild false Include Revit source excluded by XAML designer builds. DBT_IsDesignerBuild false Use normal project paths and source inclusion. _DBT_MergeDesigner true Retain public package references for DocFX's unmerged project symbols. _DBT_MergeDesigner controls package visibility separately from source inclusion. The product build merges public dependencies into their owning assemblies. DocFX reads project source, so its compilation needs those dependencies as package references. Keep the restore properties in the script aligned with the metadata properties in wiki/docfx.json. DocFX reads the projects in src/, excludes test projects, writes metadata to wiki/api/, and builds the site into wiki/_site/. Compilation errors fail the build. The conceptual script mode uses docfx-conceptual.json and builds the articles without API metadata or product builds. The reference covers the namespaces of DBTools.Core, DBTools.App, DBTools.Presentation and the tool assemblies (DBTools.GM, DBTools.SGT and others). Members without an XML comment appear without a description. Writing documentation comments Document each public type and member with /// comments. Give a <summary> for every member, a <param> for every parameter, <returns> for non-void methods and <exception> for exceptions that callers handle: /// <summary> /// Runs an action inside a Revit transaction. /// </summary> /// <param name="action">The action to run in the transaction.</param> /// <returns><see langword="true"/> if the transaction committed; otherwise <see langword="false"/>.</returns> /// <exception cref="InvalidOperationException">No document is active.</exception> public bool Execute(Action action) Use <remarks> only for constraints that a caller must know.

developer-guide/architecture/assembly-lo.title: Assembly Loading Contract | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/assembly-lo.summary: Assembly Loading Contract The product is a tree of ordinary files: one entry assembly, three top-level libraries and one assembly per tool. The installed add-in loads in Revit's default AssemblyLoadContext. Revit-hosted tests and Dev Mode load the product into a context that the dbtools-daemon creates. In every host, App loads each tool assembly by explicit path into the context that holds DBTools.dll, and Revit calls each command by its assembly path and class name. Installed layout Each supported year has one directory of ordinary files. This is the product tree that the installer, Revit-hosted test staging, Sandbox and Dev Mode use: <year>/ ├── DBTools.addin ├── DBTools.dll ├── DBTools.Core.dll ├── DBTools.Presentation.dll ├── DBTools.HandyControl.dll └── Tools/ ├── DBTools.AnalyticalSnapToLevel.dll ├── DBTools.DialogSuppression.dll ├── DBTools.ElevationTags.dll ├── DBTools.ERFT.dll ├── DBTools.FoundationTags.dll ├── DBTools.FramingJoins.dll ├── DBTools.GM.dll ├── DBTools.JoistGirderWeight.dll ├── DBTools.OrganizeFoundationTypes.dll ├── DBTools.RecordSet.dll ├── DBTools.SGT.dll ├── DBTools.Settings.dll ├── DBTools.TDV.dll └── DBTools.VTC.dll DBTools.addin names DBTools.dll and the class DBTools.App.Addin.AddinEntry. DBTools.dll contains the entry point and host infrastructure and no tool code. WPF needs the physical location of Presentation and HandyControl, so they stay at the top level. Merged libraries Every third-party runtime library is merged into one owner assembly; no third-party DLL is staged. build/Merging/AssemblyMerges.props declares the merges: App owns ricaun.Revit.UI.0.9.0. Core owns the manifest and YAML parser, MVVM, functional, tessellation, dependency injection, logging, options and primitives libraries, and Serilog.Extensions.Logging. Presentation owns the Helix and SharpDX closure, Serilog, and the public dependency injection and logging abstractions. Serilog is in Presentation, which is never reloaded, because its thread-static state must not enter a collectible load context (dotnet/runtime#134928). A declaration's Include is the assembly name. The optional PackageId names a NuGet package whose name differs; ricaun uses PackageId="ricaun.Revit.UI" because its assembly name contains a version. MSBuild passes each merge its inputs as items: the resolved runtime asset of a package, or the output of a project. The merge copies its evaluated reference files into a temporary reference directory. ILRepack searches only that directory and resolves framework identities only from those files, so other package or compiler-output files and the runtimes installed on the build host cannot change the result. MSBuild Inputs and Outputs, including the owner's project.assets.json, decide when a merge reruns. The task deletes its temporary files afterwards. App host references The pinned ricaun.Revit.UI.0.9.0 assembly references Revit 27.0.4, also when App is compiled for Revit 2026. The App merge therefore binds these host references to the exact identities of the selected year during the final Cecil normalization: RevitAPI;RevitAPIUI;AdWindows;UIFramework Only App does this. MergeReferenceGuard then resolves every TypeRef, MemberRef and attribute type name with Cecil against the selected year's evaluated references. It rejects a missing type or member, a referenced version higher than the evaluated one, and any reference to an assembly that a merge removed. The Nice3point UIFramework reference is part of the Revit reference metadata used for this check; it is not shipped. Entry and idle acknowledgement AddinEntry has a public parameterless constructor for Revit. OnStartup first calls AddinIdle.TryAcknowledge. If DBTOOLS_DAEMON_REVIT_ROLE is set to any nonempty value and the entry assembly is in exactly AssemblyLoadContext.Default, it sets the AppContext data DBToolsDaemon.IdleAddin:DBTools to the entry assembly's file location and returns Succeeded before any runtime, ribbon, logging or tool work. OnShutdown returns Succeeded immediately for that instance. Otherwise startup enters AppStartupBoundary, a non-inlined method, which starts the App lifecycle inside ToolWindowCallbackScope. Startup, shutdown and ribbon failures that cannot reach the normal log are written to %APPDATA%\DBTools\Logs\DBTools.Fallback.log with BCL APIs only. Tool resolution ToolAssemblyResolver.LoadAssembly(rootAssembly, assemblyName) loads a manifest-declared assembly. The name must be a simple name without .dll or path characters. If it equals the root assembly's name, the root is returned. Otherwise the resolver: requires a file-backed root assembly; resolves <root directory>/Tools/<assemblyName>.dll and requires the file; reads the file's assembly name and requires the declared simple name; returns an assembly of that name already loaded in the root's context, if its full identity and location match the file; a different identity or location is an error; otherwise loads the file with that context's LoadFromAssemblyPath. The resolver does not search other contexts, install an AppDomain resolver or create a load context. The ribbon registers each command by its assembly location, full class name and availability type name. Availability is implemented by the command's own assembly. Command and availability callbacks enter ToolWindowCallbackScope, which suppresses ExecutionContext flow and sets contextual reflection to the command's load context. Hosted tests and Dev Mode The daemon creates ProductLoadContext for hosted tests and DevModeLoadContext for Dev Mode. App loads each declared tool from Tools/ into that context; Dev Mode does not probe other subfolders. Presentation and HandyControl stay loaded for the life of the process. App, Core and the tool assemblies can be reloaded, as the host decides. Sandbox Sandbox runs one new process in the default context for each candidate year. Its entry point uses only BCL types: it validates the candidate, loads the top-level product files and the Tools/ assemblies from their paths, and then starts WPF through a non-inlined method. The process exits after validation, so no candidate assembly remains loaded for the next year. See Sandbox Validator. Distribution hashes Distribution validation checks the exact relative file set, PE identities, source-derived versions, first-party reference identities, file lengths and SHA-256 hashes. The hashes identify the staged candidate. Nothing checks them when an assembly loads. See Build Pipeline, Project References and Installation.

developer-guide/architecture/build-pipel.title: Build Pipeline | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/build-pipel.summary: Build Pipeline build.sh (Linux, WSL) and build.ps1 (Windows, PowerShell 7) are the build entry points. Both run dotnet build build/Build.proj -t:<Target> with the pinned SDK; a plain dotnet build build/Build.proj -t:<Target> runs the same graph. The default target is BuildAll, which builds, validates and publishes the complete distribution for Revit 2026 and 2027. BuildAll compiles no test projects. Synopsis ./build.sh [Target] [parameters] pwsh -NoProfile -File build.ps1 [Target] [parameters] Both entries print build/Usage.txt for --help. Option names ignore dashes and case. Option Short form Description --Configuration <Release\|Debug> -d, --debug Build configuration; -d selects Debug --Years <years> -y, --year Revit years, for example 2026 or "2026 2027" --SkipClean <true\|false> --clean --clean sets SkipClean to false and deletes build output first --Verbose [true\|false] -v, --verbose; -q, --quiet Terminal verbosity; quiet is the default --DryRun [true\|false] BuildBundle and BuildInstaller skip the bundle and print the ISCC command instead of running it --CandidateDistributionPath <dir> --candidate-dist Package an existing promoted tree --InnoSetupExe <path> Inno Setup compiler for BuildInstaller --Revit2026Dir <dir>, --Revit2027Dir <dir> Installed Revit, used only for validation --TestProjects <a,b> Projects for the selected-test targets An unknown option exits with status 2 before any SDK work, with Unknown build parameter '<option>'. The target is the first positional argument. build.sh rejects the NUKE options --target, --root, --solution, --continue, --nologo, --verbosity, --plan, --profile, --skip and --host with a message that starts ERROR: '<option>' is a NUKE option, and this build does not use NUKE. build.sh exits with status 3 in a Windows shell (Git Bash, Cygwin) and names build.ps1. Build.proj validates the option values in its Initialize step: a boolean other than true or false fails before any target runs. Targets Target Result BuildAll Complete 2026/2027 build, validation and promotion to .artifacts/dist/Release BuildApp [-y <year>] App, Core, Presentation, HandyControl and the tool assemblies ValidatePrePush BuildApp plus manifest type validation BuildTests [-y <year>] Every test project and the hosted product inputs; all years by default BuildSelectedLocalTests, BuildSelectedPureTests, BuildSelectedDesignAutomationTests The projects named by --TestProjects in one test lane AssembleDistributionCandidate [-y <year>] A candidate year tree for checks that consume one; it is not published StagePortableAcceptanceInput Stage the candidate and Revit references for portable validation ValidateDistributionCandidate Portable validation and Dev Mode preflight of the candidate PackageSandboxValidationInput A content-addressed zip of the candidate and Sandbox for Windows validation PromoteToDist Replace the published distribution with the validated candidate BuildBundle Package the promoted tree into .artifacts/bundle/DBTools.bundle, one year tree per Revit year, under the Version.props product version BuildInstaller Build the bundle, then the installer with Inno Setup ValidateManifestTypes, VerifyArtifacts, BuildSandbox, BuildValidationRunner, Restore, Clean, Info Individual steps BuildAll, StagePortableAcceptanceInput, ValidateDistributionCandidate, PackageSandboxValidationInput, PromoteToDist, BuildBundle and BuildInstaller build the complete distribution. They require the Release configuration and the complete supported year set, which is the default; a -y that omits a supported year fails. ValidateDistributionCandidate and PromoteToDist also require a clean Git worktree. BuildBundle and BuildInstaller with --candidate-dist PATH package an existing promoted tree without building. --clean deletes build output; without it, an incremental BuildAll reuses the existing artifacts. No target switches to another SDK or output root. BuildAll depends on PromoteToDist, so it runs, in order: Restore, BuildValidationRunner (the Dev Mode policy runner), BuildApp for each year with ValidateProductVersions, VerifyArtifacts, StageDistributionCandidate, WriteCandidateMetadata, StagePortableAcceptanceInput, ValidateDistributionCandidate, ValidateManifestTypes and PromoteToDist. Examples ./build.sh BuildAll ./build.sh BuildAll --clean ./build.sh BuildApp --Configuration Debug --Years 2026 ./build.sh BuildTests ./build.sh BuildSelectedLocalTests --TestProjects DBTools.App.Local.Tests -y 2026 pwsh -NoProfile -File build.ps1 BuildAll Individual projects also build with plain dotnet build. Their MSBuild graph computes content versions and stages runtime prerequisites, but does not validate or publish a distribution. Implementation Each entry maps its options to MSBuild properties, acquires the pinned SDK, initializes the HandyControl submodule when needed, and runs Build.proj. Both entries produce the same dotnet build command line. No Build.proj target runs bash or Python, so BuildAll and BuildTests behave the same on Windows. Test execution is done by test.sh. Build.proj owns the target graph and starts each child dotnet build with its own binary log. The C# code of each target is a BuildPipelineStep in build/Tasks (DBTools.Build.Tasks, net8.0, loaded by the SDK's MSBuild on .NET 10). It owns option validation, Revit reference checks, Inno Setup discovery and the distribution steps. The task assembly is written to .artifacts/build-tasks/<Configuration>/ and recompiles only when its inputs change. Compilation on every operating system uses the centrally pinned Nice3point Revit API metadata packages with runtime assets excluded. An installed Revit is never a build prerequisite. --Revit2026Dir and --Revit2027Dir name an installation, native or mounted under WSL, for validation only. The staged Revit API files are reference metadata, not an executable runtime. APS Design Automation builds the separate Revit 2026 net8.0 Sentinel test project with its own API provider. Product output build/MSBuild/ProductOutput.proj and ProductOutput.targets stage the product tree for each year in .artifacts/bin/Release/<year>/net10.0-windows/. StageProductOutputTask keeps the Tools/ directory and validates each declared owner image. Intermediate runtime inputs can be year-keyed under .artifacts/bin/Release/<year>-runtime-input/. Local test staging copies the year tree recursively into the test output and removes stale top-level tool images. The installer receives the file list from DistributionContract.ProductFiles as the ISCC define ProductFiles and checks each year against it. Assembly merges build/Merging/AssemblyMerges.props declares one owner for each merged library; AssemblyMerge.targets runs the merge. Every merged library is private to its owner and absent from the year tree, including Tools/. Each owner is merged once per build; MSBuild Inputs and Outputs skip the merge when nothing changed. The merger writes a deterministic MVID and PDB, and version validation requires each stable assembly (Presentation, HandyControl) to have the same version and SHA-256 in every year. Owner Merged libraries DBTools.dll (App) ricaun.Revit.UI DBTools.Core DBTools.Manifest, YamlDotNet, CommunityToolkit.Mvvm, CSharpFunctionalExtensions, LibTessDotNet, Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection, .Logging, .Options, .Primitives, Serilog.Extensions.Logging DBTools.Presentation HelixToolkit and SharpDX assemblies, Cyotek.Drawing.BitmapFont, CommunityToolkit.Diagnostics, Serilog, Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions, Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Abstractions Serilog is in Presentation, which is never reloaded, because its thread-static state must not enter a collectible load context (dotnet/runtime#134928). The merge details are in Assembly Loading Contract. Content versions WPF resolves compiled resource URIs by assembly name and version, and Dev Mode identifies Presentation and HandyControl by full identity and SHA-256 hash. A content version therefore changes exactly when an assembly image can change. build/MSBuild/ContentVersion.targets computes it inside each ordinary compilation from these inputs: source, XAML and resource bytes, with the metadata that names, types and exposes each resource (Link, LogicalName, ManifestResourceName, Access, culture and generator metadata); resolved references: a package by its immutable coordinates, a project or local reference by its bytes, resolved before WPF markup compilation; source generators and the properties visible to them; the emitted assembly attributes, rendered as the SDK generates them, and the framework attribute; the signing key, Win32 manifest and resources, and the effective PathMap; the compiler options that change emitted code or metadata; for a merge owner, the merged project images and the merger code and binaries; for HandyControl, its vendor URI rewrite rules and the rewrite task's source (DBT_ContentVersionRule and DBT_ContentVersionInput). The content hash keys the rewrite, and a missing rewritten file reruns it. These are not inputs: build scripts and targets, .editorconfig and other analyzer configuration, diagnostic-only analyzers and warning options. Editing them changes no version. No Git commit or tree enters assembly attributes, content inputs or debug metadata. The computation runs inside the project's own compilation: it starts no second MSBuild evaluation and loads no other project. Because the inputs are hashed, resetting a source timestamp cannot hide changed bytes. A referenced content version is part of the referencing image, so consumers change version with it. An implementation-only change behind an unchanged version does not propagate through compiler references. The input list is written one entry per line to: .artifacts/obj/content-version/<Configuration>/<year|shared>-<flavor>/<project>/<framework>/inputs.txt The SHA-256 of the list is the input hash. Its first six bytes give the four-part assembly version: 4.<u16(bytes 0..1) % 65535>.<u16(bytes 2..3) % 65535>.<u16(bytes 4..5) % 65535> AssemblyInformationalVersion is <version>+inputs.<hash>. Compare two input lists to see why a version changed. Identical inputs keep the same identity and output timestamps. Content versions apply to Presentation, HandyControl, Core, App and projects that set DBT_IsToolAssembly=true. Other product metadata uses the release version from Version.props. Checked-in files are named relative to the repository root and artifacts relative to a relocatable root, so a fresh clone gives the same versions. Repository source and intermediate PDB documents use the path prefix /_/dbtools/; transformed vendor documents use /_/dbtools/vendor-build/. SourceLink revision stamping is off. A WPF temporary project hashes its parent's input list, so local-type identities in BAML carry the final version. The staged year trees carry the version evidence: each first-party image has its content version and input hash, the version must derive from that hash, and a stable image must be byte-identical in every year. The staging step reads them before it validates the compiled resource URIs. Candidate validation and promotion Distribution validation walks each year tree recursively. It requires the exact relative file set with Tools/ as the only directory, and checks PE identities, source-derived versions, first-party reference identities, framework references, and the length and SHA-256 of every file. It also checks the add-in entry, commands, availability types, manifests, resources and ownership. A missing, extra, misnamed, misplaced or stale file fails the candidate. Manifest validation scans every manifest.yml under src/ and resolves module, command, availability and design-time ViewModel type names against the compiled images of each year. Every declared owner must resolve to Tools/<owner>.dll. BuildAll and ValidatePrePush run it. ValidateDistributionCandidate prints one Dev Mode preflight line per year: Revit <year> Dev Mode preflight: <n> failures, <m> warnings; outcome=<x> Promotion requires a clean Git worktree (tracked and untracked files) with a resolved HEAD. Three records describe a distribution: The build metadata (build.json) records the years, frameworks, the distribution fingerprint, the Git commit and tree IDs, the source versions, the hash of each product file and the Protocol package pin. The portable acceptance receipt, written by ValidateDistributionCandidate, records for each year the validated files, the Revit reference descriptors and the Dev Mode preflight result. The promotion receipt, .artifacts/dist/Release/promotion-receipt.json, embeds the acceptance receipt with the source snapshot and the distribution fingerprint. It contains no temporary staging paths; consumers validate it against the published tree. Promotion validates the staged candidate, its fingerprint, the exact year trees and the receipt. It then deletes the published .artifacts/build.json, replaces .artifacts/dist/Release with the validated tree, and writes build.json last. Read the distribution only after the build command exits successfully. When promotion prepares the new tree, each declared file whose SHA-256 equals the file at the same path in the current .artifacts/dist/Release becomes a hard link to that file; new and changed files are copied. An unchanged file therefore stays the same file across promotions, and a virus scanner that has scanned it (Windows Defender on a Dev Mode host) does not scan it again. If the platform refuses a link (different file system, no hard-link support, permission error), promotion logs the reason once at low importance and copies that file and all remaining files. No step writes into a published file. Point Dev Mode at .artifacts/dist/Release/<year> directly; a copy is a set of new files that the scanner scans again. Revit-hosted test inputs Staging for Revit-hosted tests builds one complete product tree for the selected year and includes it with relative paths unchanged, including the 14 tool assemblies in Tools/. Test assemblies, NUnit and adapter files, and companions are separate inputs. The input cache checks relative path, identity, length and hash before the daemon request is written. Test restore roots are per year: each year of the local scope restores separately, and Design Automation tests share the 2026 root. The Pure root restores every Pure project against $(DBT_PureRevitYear) owners through static graph restore. NuGet keys package specifications by project path, so one root never mixes owner variants. See Test Pipeline. Pinned SDK build/DotNet/sdk.sh selects the SDK version from global.json. If no installed dotnet has that SDK, it uses the private root ~/.dotnet/pinned-sdk-<version>. A system dotnet with the pinned SDK is used as is. A build needs only the SDK. A net8.0 test host (the APS Design Automation Sentinel) also needs the .NET 8 runtime. sdk.sh pins that runtime version, because global.json cannot, and installs it only when such a host runs: test.sh requests it, or run bash build/DotNet/sdk.sh --test-host-runtime. On a system dotnet without the .NET 8 runtime, a net8.0 test host uses the private root. A package in the private root is valid only when its marker file, .dbt-complete-<package>-<version>, names its archive. To install a package, sdk.sh: checks the archive against the SHA-512 in Microsoft's release metadata; extracts it into a staging directory beside the root; renames the version directories into place; writes the marker. A version directory without a valid marker is replaced from the verified archive; one that already matches stays. The lock <root>.lock serializes installs across builds and worktrees, and a build that waited for the lock checks the markers again before it installs anything. The Linux installer requires Python 3.10 or later. build.ps1 uses the same root, SHA-512 check, marker and lock for the SDK without Python. It downloads the release metadata's dotnet-sdk-win-<arch>.zip and replaces a root without a valid marker as a whole. It installs no test-host runtime. Build servers DBT_BUILD_SERVERS sets the server mode for every wrapper invocation (build.sh, test.sh, the lane helpers and their child builds). DBT_MSBUILD_MAX_CPU_COUNT sets the graph build parallelism (default 2); the wrappers validate it and Build.proj passes it to its child builds. build.sh runs Build.proj itself without the MSBuild server; each child dotnet build uses the selected mode. 1 (default): the invocation owns one compiler server and one MSBuild server. Its scope ID, dbtools-scope-<owner pid>-<run id>, is the compiler pipe name, and <scope id>-msbuild is the MSBuild handshake salt. On every trapped exit, each server gets a shutdown request with a 30 s timeout; then every process the invocation still owns is terminated, the compiler by its exact -pipename: argument and MSBuild nodes by the exact salt in their environment. No process is matched by name. A starting invocation stops dbtools-scope servers whose owner process no longer exists; servers of a live owner are never touched. The servers make a clean build faster and raise its peak memory use. 0: no compiler server and no MSBuild server (UseSharedCompilation=false). Use this on hosts that admit builds by free memory. build.ps1 always uses mode 0, because the ownership checks read Linux /proc. Node reuse is off in both modes. Outside a wrapper, Directory.Build.props keeps the compiler server off. UseSharedCompilation is not a content-version input. build/Testing/check-build-server-lifecycle.sh <second-checkout> runs the server lifecycle with the real SDK: a normal exit, a failed build, SIGTERM, SIGKILL followed by the next build's sweep, and a concurrent owner in another checkout. Run it manually. Logs Each run writes to .artifacts/build/<YYYYMMDD-HHmmssfff>-<pid>/, named by build.sh or build.ps1 (by Build.proj for a plain dotnet build). The folder holds the full plain-text console.log at detailed verbosity and one binary log per child build. When the build ends, successfully or not, the entry writes a completed marker and copies the log to .artifacts/build/console.log. Each run first prunes old folders. It keeps the ten newest completed folders, deletes folders that contain only a marker, deletes unmarked folders after 24 hours without activity, and skips folders whose process is still running. Test builds write .artifacts/build/test-matrix.binlog, replacing the previous one. The terminal shows per-step progress, errors, warnings, the Dev Mode preflight lines and the MSBuild summary. --verbose adds the child build output. The file log is always detailed. Directory layout Path Contents .artifacts/bin/<Configuration>/<Year>/<TFM>/ Compiler output; the shared bucket when no year is selected .artifacts/obj/ Intermediate output and content-version input lists .artifacts/vendor/<Configuration>/handycontrol/net10.0-windows/ HandyControl build output .artifacts/sandbox/<Configuration>/<year>/<TFM>/ Sandbox build output .artifacts/.staging/<build id>/distribution-candidate/Release/ Candidate distribution .artifacts/dist/Release/<year>/ Published distribution, with promotion-receipt.json in .artifacts/dist/Release/ .artifacts/build.json Build metadata of the published distribution .artifacts/bundle/, .artifacts/installer/ Bundle and installer .artifacts/build/ Run logs Directory.Build.props defines the output and object roots. WPF temporary projects (_wpftmp) get a separate intermediate path. The standard target framework is net10.0-windows; Design Automation uses net8.0-windows. Directory.Build.targets adds host warnings, project-reference routing, WPF designer fixes and product and test staging hooks. HandyControl HandyControl is built from the vendor/HandyControl submodule through build/HandyControl/DBTools.HandyControl.csproj. The project imports the four upstream shared .projitems files and the upstream resources, writes transformed intermediate copies that use the DBTools assembly name and versioned pack URIs, and compiles Shared/Themes/Theme.xaml as the theme. The upstream project-root Theme.xaml generated by its PreBuild step is not an input. A missing submodule, resource or transform input fails with its path. Concurrency Run one build or test command per worktree at a time. Concurrent builds need separate BaseArtifactsDir roots; sharing compiler or WPF output between roots is not supported. A nested test command reuses the build-server scope of its parent. build.sh, build.ps1 and test.sh take no lock and do not check free memory. Continuous integration The CI and Documentation workflows run only on manual dispatch, not on pushes or pull requests. CI mode build runs BuildAll; mode build-test also builds and runs the selected tests. The Documentation workflow publishes the site through the wiki server. The release workflow, triggered by a published release, builds and promotes the distribution and bundle on Linux, then runs only the Inno Setup compiler on Windows. The self-hosted Windows test runner consumes compiled test artifacts through test.sh and does not build the product. Source maps and CANON These checks are run by the pre-push hook and CI, not by any build target: python3 .agents/work/canon_source_maps.py writes one MAP.md beside each manifest. A map lists the current source tree, including untracked files that are not ignored, and labels test folders as test mirrors. --check recomputes the maps byte for byte (UTF-8, LF) and fails if one is stale. python3 .agents/work/canon_source_fidelity.py --gate checks folder and namespace agreement, type and file identity, repeated declarations, vocabulary and unresolved rulings for the declared source roots. Troubleshooting Problem Action dotnet or the pinned SDK is missing Run bash build/DotNet/sdk.sh. The .NET 8 runtime for the Design Automation Sentinel is missing Run bash build/DotNet/sdk.sh --test-host-runtime. HandyControl output is missing Run the build from a Git checkout with network access, so the entry can initialize the submodule. WPF designer output collides Build through the repository targets, so _wpftmp gets its own intermediate path. MSBuild task DLLs stay locked A wrapper killed past its exit trap leaves its servers running until the next wrapper invocation stops them. Run the command again. A focused build is slow Build the project or use BuildApp; keep BuildAll for the full distribution. See Project References, Test Pipeline, Assembly Loading Contract and Sandbox Validator.

developer-guide/architecture/overview.ht.title: Architecture Overview | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/overview.ht.summary: Architecture Overview DB Tools is a suite of Revit add-in tools. Revit loads one entry assembly, DBTools.dll, built from src/DBTools.App. App loads shared infrastructure from DBTools.Core.dll, stable WPF types from DBTools.Presentation.dll, and each tool from its own assembly in the Tools/ directory. flowchart TB Revit[Revit Host] -->|DBTools.addin| App[DBTools.dll / App] App --> Core[DBTools.Core.dll] App --> Presentation[DBTools.Presentation.dll] Presentation --> Handy[DBTools.HandyControl.dll] App -->|explicit path: Tools/| Tools[Tool assemblies] Core --> RevitAPI[Revit API] Components Project Assembly Responsibility src/DBTools.App DBTools.dll Revit entry point, startup and shutdown, service composition, ribbon, embedded tool manifests src/DBTools.Core DBTools.Core.dll Shared execution (call gate, transactions, safe execution), settings, logging, tool registry, manifest loading, tool assembly resolution src/DBTools.Presentation DBTools.Presentation.dll WPF resources, themes, controls and window shells that live for the whole Revit process build/HandyControl DBTools.HandyControl.dll Renamed build of the vendored HandyControl library src/Tools/<Category>/<Tool> DBTools.<Tool>.dll One tool: its module, commands, features and views src/DBTools.Sandbox Sandbox executable Candidate validator and UI development host that runs without Revit Presentation references only WPF and HandyControl. App, Core and the tools may reference Presentation. See Project References. Each window merges the theme into its own resources, not into Application.Resources, so DB Tools does not change other add-ins. See Theme System. Product tree Each supported Revit year has one directory with DBTools.addin, the four top-level assemblies and the 14 tool assemblies in Tools/; see Installed layout. The build merges every third-party runtime library into one owner assembly, so the directory contains no other DLLs. The installer, Revit-hosted test staging, Sandbox and Dev Mode use the same tree. See Build Pipeline. Load contexts The installed add-in runs in Revit's default AssemblyLoadContext. For Revit-hosted tests and Dev Mode, the dbtools-daemon loads the product into its own context (ProductLoadContext or DevModeLoadContext). DB Tools creates no load context of its own. App loads each tool assembly into the context that already holds DBTools.dll. Startup DBTools.App.Addin.AddinEntry implements IExternalApplication. OnStartup runs these steps in order: Idle check. If DBTOOLS_DAEMON_REVIT_ROLE is set and the entry assembly is in the default load context, the add-in sets the AppContext key DBToolsDaemon.IdleAddin:DBTools to the entry assembly's location and returns Succeeded without further work. OnShutdown then also returns immediately. This lets the daemon run a Revit that has the installed add-in while it tests its own copy. Callback scope. AppStartupBoundary (not inlined) enters ToolWindowCallbackScope, which suppresses ExecutionContext flow and sets contextual reflection to the entry assembly's load context. Runtime. App reads the Revit year from VersionNumber, creates the logging host and the service provider, and publishes them through AppRuntimeAccessor. Theme validation. ThemeValidator.ValidateOrThrow loads and freezes the theme dictionaries and lays out a probe control tree. Ribbon. App composes the ribbon from the embedded manifests. Background startup. App starts the local Revit task host and an asynchronous startup task that installs the Revit main-window owner provider and attaches tool hooks. Publication. App registers an Idling handler for failed-startup cleanup, then the deferred startup handlers (ApplicationInitialized and Idling), and publishes the started state. A failure in steps 3 to 6 cleans up what was created and returns Failed. A failure of the background task is cleaned up on the next Idling event. Failures that cannot reach the normal log are written to %APPDATA%\DBTools\Logs\DBTools.Fallback.log with BCL APIs only, so this log works before Core loads. Tools and commands Each tool has a manifest.yml that names its assembly, module type, commands and availability types. App embeds all manifests. At startup: ToolModuleCatalog loads and validates the embedded manifests once. The App registrar loads each declared assembly with ToolAssemblyResolver.LoadAssembly, which loads only <entry directory>/Tools/<name>.dll. The registrar creates each module, collects its settings, services, settings packs and hooks, checks ownership, and merges them into the App service collection. Manifests without a module register only ribbon items. ToolRegistry.MergeFrom validates every incoming tool and hook against the existing registrations before it changes anything, so a conflict leaves the registry unchanged. Duplicate internal names are rejected. The ribbon refers to each command by its assembly location and full type name. When a command runs, CommandPreflight checks, before any run scope exists, that its ribbon panel is enabled in Settings, that its availability type allows it, and that no active feature warning disables it. Only then does CommandContextFactory create the run scope with the command's execution profile. Settings-only and hook-only tools still have a manifest and a module. Services and scopes The App service provider holds application-lifetime services: logging, settings, hooks, ISafeExecutor, the tool registry and ribbon state. Each command run, modeless session or test opens a scope that holds the Revit run scope (IRevitRunScope), its IRevitCallGate, ITransactionRunner and ITransactionGroupService. Command, availability and window callbacks enter ToolWindowCallbackScope. Source layout Tool source is under src/Tools/<Category>/<Tool>/ with namespace root DBTools.<Tool>. Folders are named for what they own, for example App/, Features/, Domain/, Revit/, Settings/, Assets/ and Tests/. A tool has only the folders it needs. Generic folders such as Helpers, Models or Infrastructure are not used for production code. Supported years Desktop Revit 2026 (2026.5 or later) and Revit 2027 both target net10.0-windows. build/Distribution/RevitYearContract.cs defines the supported years. APS Design Automation tests use a separate Revit 2026 net8.0-windows profile. Build and validation build.sh (Linux, WSL) and build.ps1 (Windows) run build/Build.proj. BuildAll builds, validates and publishes the complete two-year distribution. BuildApp, BuildTests and test.sh build smaller graphs. See Build Pipeline and Test Pipeline. Distribution validation records the length and SHA-256 of every file in the candidate. These hashes identify what was built and tested. They do not authenticate assemblies at load time.

developer-guide/architecture/project-ref.title: Project References | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/project-ref.summary: Project References Desktop Revit 2026 (2026.5 or later) and Revit 2027 use one target framework, net10.0-windows. build/Distribution/RevitYearContract.cs and build/MSBuild/RevitTargetFrameworks.props define the supported years and their framework. Projects use $(DBT_RevitTargetFramework) and contain no year-specific framework conditions. Assemblies Project Assembly Role src/DBTools.App DBTools.dll Revit entry point, App lifecycle and host infrastructure, embedded tool manifests src/DBTools.Core DBTools.Core.dll Shared execution, settings, logging, tool registry, manifest loading, tool assembly resolution src/DBTools.Presentation DBTools.Presentation.dll Stable WPF resources, controls and window shells build/HandyControl DBTools.HandyControl.dll Renamed HandyControl build src/DBTools.Manifest merged into Core Portable manifest.yml parser (net8.0) for build tooling and validation src/Tools/<Category>/<Tool> DBTools.<Tool>.dll One tool: commands, features and tool services src/DBTools.Sandbox Sandbox executable Candidate validation and UI development without Revit Reference direction App references Core and Presentation. It embeds every src/Tools/**/manifest.yml as a resource and compiles no tool source. Core references Presentation and DBTools.Manifest. It references the Revit API where a shared capability needs it. Tools reference Core, and Presentation for their UI. Presentation references only WPF and HandyControl. It does not reference App, Core, tool types or the Revit API. Sandbox compiles against Core, Presentation and HandyControl without copying their runtime files, and loads them from the candidate year directory at run time. App owns the ricaun.Revit.UI compile reference; the merge folds its runtime into DBTools.dll. Add a third-party runtime dependency through a declared merge in build/Merging/AssemblyMerges.props, not through a copy step. See Assembly Loading Contract. Tool assemblies Set DBT_IsToolAssembly=true in a project that produces a shipped tool assembly. The build stages its output in the year's Tools/ directory and gives it a content-derived version. At run time App resolves the tool through ToolAssemblyResolver, which loads into the context of the App and Core root assembly. The same rule applies in the default context, in the daemon's ProductLoadContext and in DevModeLoadContext. Every manifest under src/Tools/ has its own assembly, including Settings, SGT and DialogSuppression. A tool assembly must not contain a copy of Core or of Presentation. Test references Pure projects use the ordinary compile and runtime graph of their scope. Revit-hosted (.Local.Tests) projects receive the selected year's host references and the staged product tree with Tools/ intact. Input generation for Revit-hosted tests keeps the product root separate from test assemblies and adapter dependencies. A project reference must not place product assemblies flat beside a test assembly: the product requires the year root and its Tools/ subdirectory. Keep a dependency's host or resource constraint in the project that owns it, and validate the resulting candidate tree. Do not add projects for unsupported frameworks or a second load context for DB Tools. See Assembly Loading Contract, Build Pipeline and Test Pipeline.

developer-guide/architecture/revit-execu.title: Revit Execution and Progress Overlay | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/revit-execu.summary: Revit Execution and Progress Overlay DB Tools runs all Revit API work through a call gate, inside a run scope that each command, modeless session or test owns. Tool windows report long operations through the progress overlay. This page owns the design of run scopes, call gates, transaction services and the progress overlay. DBTools.Core describes the rest of the Core library and its source folders. Command entry ToolCommand (src/DBTools.Core/Tools/Commands/ToolCommand.cs) is the base class of every Revit command. Its public Execute runs the command body inside ISafeExecutor and gives the protected RunAsync hook one owning CommandContext; see ToolCommand for the API. Command subclasses resolve services from ICommandContext. Its base interface IAppRunScope exposes the scope's RevitRunScope and Resolve<T>(). A feature that owns a window composes ToolWindowFactory and calls IToolWindowSession.ShowDialog() or Show(). The session owns the reflection scope and the window's retirement. An expected refusal throws SafeExecutionRefusedException with a reason for the user. SafeExecutor then returns SafeExecutionStatus.Refused, with no failure surface and no exception diagnostics. SafeExecutionRefusalReporter shows a Warning banner, which writes the one Warning log entry; an execution without a banner logs [Refused] {Name}: {Message}. ToolCommand returns Revit Result.Cancelled for a refusal and for a failure. An unexpected exception writes Error diagnostics and shows an Error banner. Run scopes App composition (AppServiceProviderFactory) registers IAppRunScopeFactory with the Core implementation AppRunScopeFactory. CommandContextFactory calls Create(UIApplication, AppRunScopeProfile). The factory selects the call gate for the profile, constructs RevitRunScope, and returns the concrete AppRunScope, which owns scoped service resolution, its IRevitRunScope and disposal. Construction and disposal keep the primary failure, attempt every owned cleanup step and report further cleanup failures in order. Profile Call gate Use InlineUi (default) InlineRevitCallGate Modal commands and daemon-hosted Revit automation that already run on the Revit UI thread. QueuedModeless QueuedRevitCallGate Modeless tool windows and long workflows that must queue Revit API work to the UI thread through the App-owned ExternalEvent host. A tool selects its profile through RunProfile in its manifest; ToolRegistration uses InlineUi when none is given. IRevitRunScope owns the UIApplication, the call gate, document access and disposal. Transaction services are scoped registrations, resolved with Resolve<T>() on IAppRunScope or ICommandContext. public interface IRevitRunScope : IDisposable { UIApplication UIApplication { get; } IRevitCallGate CallGate { get; } UIDocument GetActiveUiDocument(); Document GetActiveDocument(); Document GetVerifiedActiveDocument(Document expectedDocument, string? context = null); } A consumer that keeps its launch document calls GetVerifiedActiveDocument(...). The run scope rejects an invalid expected or active document and requires matching DocumentSessionKey values before it returns the active document. RevitServiceCollectionExtensions registers only the Revit-scoped run-scope access, the call gate and the transaction services. The App composition root registers IAppRunScopeFactory, safe execution, command preflight and the command context services. Call gates IRevitCallGate is the single entry point for Revit API access. It runs synchronous callbacks on the Revit UI thread. Revit API calls outside the call gate can raise invalid-context exceptions or break UI-thread rules. public interface IRevitCallGate { bool InGate { get; } Task<T> RunAsync<T>(Func<UIApplication, T> work, CancellationToken ct = default, RevitCallGateMode mode = RevitCallGateMode.Auto); Task RunAsync(Action<UIApplication> work, CancellationToken ct = default, RevitCallGateMode mode = RevitCallGateMode.Auto); } Mode Behavior Auto Run inline when the caller already has a gate context; otherwise queue through the owned ExternalEvent host. ForceQueue Always queue through the owned ExternalEvent, in a later turn. The inline gate rejects it with ContextUnavailableException. InlineRevitCallGate(UIApplication) runs delegates immediately on the Revit UI thread with the supplied application. Modal commands use it. QueuedRevitCallGate schedules the callback through its ExternalEvent host. QueuedRevitCallGate and the host's RevitCallGateTask each require an ILogger from their composition owner; App passes its runtime logger to AppLocalRevitTaskLifecycle.Start. A missing logger is a construction error. The active UIApplication, the queued-gate depth and the Revit-test depth are internal scoped state. QueuedRevitCallGate owns the queued and test scopes; RevitRunScope owns its application context token. Every scope restores the exact previous value, and a repeated disposal does nothing. Delegate admission Admission is synchronous and runs before the gate validates the API context or schedules anything. Keep asynchronous workflows outside the gate and make in-gate delegates synchronous: await _gate.RunAsync(app => { // Revit API work here (synchronous only) return true; }); Every member of an Action invocation list is checked for an async state machine, so an async void action is rejected. A delegate whose result type is Task, Task<T>, ValueTask or ValueTask<T>, including nullable ValueTask, is rejected. A multicast result delegate with a reference result type is rejected, because ordinary multicast dispatch exposes only the last return value. After invocation, a reference-typed result gets a runtime Task/ValueTask check, which also finds interface-typed Task and boxed ValueTask values. Custom awaiter structs are not detected. Sources: src/DBTools.Core/Revit/Execution/CallGate/{CallGateDelegateValidator,InlineRevitCallGate,QueuedRevitCallGate,RevitCallGateTask,RevitCallGateTaskQueue}.cs. API-context admission RevitCallGateApiContext.IsActive decides whether the current code has Revit API context. Known native entry points use the internal synchronous Enter scope. An untracked call first checks the Revit dispatcher thread, then creates and immediately disposes an unraised ExternalEvent with a stateless no-op handler. Worker threads return false before the probe. Every untracked call probes again. No result is cached across turns. Current exposes a known UIApplication only while the context is active. An ambient application reference does not grant API context. The public UIApplication constructor requires ApplicationServices.Application; there is no public conversion from UIControlledApplication.ControlledApplication. If startup has not received a UIApplication, queued work gets one from the real ExternalEvent callback. No private-field reflection is used. The probe creates a new event instead of adding and removing a handler on a Revit event. It does not change the subscriber collection of the current event and does not write a document, so it is legal in Idling, ViewActivated, DocumentChanged and updater callbacks. Admission does not permit an API that a particular callback forbids; callers must obey read-only and dynamic-update restrictions. The 2026 and 2027 API references list the Create signature and the null-handler exception, but not the outside-context exception. An Autodesk forum thread describes that runtime check and the difference between UI-thread access and API context. The probe does not identify which add-in owns a callback. Inside another add-in's main-thread API callback it returns true, and DB Tools runs inline without its own scope. Callbacks that DB Tools owns enter an explicit synchronous UIApplication scope; later continuations must probe or queue again. The scope is a ref struct, so a caller cannot hold it across an await. Its shared lifetime lets a wrong-thread disposal revoke the context before the misuse is reported. Enter is internal; App's native callbacks and FoundationTags' Idling owner use it. GM has access for synchronous-delegate validation only and does not enter scopes. Queued turns Each native Execute turn of the queued gate runs, in FIFO order, every item that was waiting when the turn started. N waiting calls cost one Revit round trip. Items queued during a turn wait for the next turn. After the first item, a turn starts no new item once its 50 ms budget (RevitCallGateTask.DrainBudget) is used. A failed or canceled item completes its own task; the turn continues with the next item. An item that leaves a transaction open in any document ends the turn. Revit discards what a callback leaves open only when the callback returns, so the next item must run in a later turn. An item that creates a transaction group through RevitTransactionGroups.Begin also ends the turn. Nested Auto calls run inline. ForceQueue defers to a later turn. A caller that needs several reads for one user action makes them in one RunAsync body, or starts independent calls together so that one turn runs them all. A transaction group without an open transaction is not visible to the open-transaction check. Production code therefore creates every TransactionGroup through RevitTransactionGroups.Begin(document, name, validateStart). The factory calls RevitCallGateTurnBoundary.EndAfterCurrentCall(), so the current turn ends when the running call returns, then constructs and starts the group and disposes it if the start fails. The build contract suite (TransactionGroupTurnBoundaryContractTests) inspects the compiled production assemblies and rejects TransactionGroup construction outside that factory. The scheduler posts every raise to the Revit dispatcher at Normal priority, also from the dispatcher thread. A caller never waits on native Raise, a burst of calls shares one raise, and the raise for work left after a turn runs after Execute returns. Denied and TimedOut raise results keep the queue and retry with a backoff from 50 ms, doubling to at most 500 ms, for at most 5 seconds (RevitCallGateRaiseRetry). When that time expires, the waiting batch faults; the scheduler still accepts new work. Each turn feeds a Debug summary with the prefix [CallGate/Turns]: turns and calls, maximum queue depth, the Raise-to-Execute gap, Execute duration, native Raise duration and results, and refused-raise retries. The summary is written when a turn leaves the queue empty, at most once per second, or after 10 s of a queue that stays busy. Turns inside the one-second interval are reported with the next activity. Retirement cancels the posted raise, stops and detaches the retry timer, releases queued delegates and disposes the native event. Dropped tasks never complete, so a worker that waits synchronously on one hangs. Cleanup after a failed startup cancels the tasks instead, because Revit and its callers are still running. Transactions Resolve transaction services from the command scope: context.Resolve<ITransactionRunner>() and context.Resolve<ITransactionGroupService>(). RevitServiceCollectionExtensions registers both as scoped services on the scope's IRevitCallGate. ITransactionRunner public interface ITransactionRunner { Task RunInActiveDocumentAsync(string name, Action<RevitTransactionContext> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<T> RunInActiveDocumentAsync<T>(string name, Func<RevitTransactionContext, T> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task RunInDocumentAsync(Document doc, string name, Action<RevitTransactionContext> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<T> RunInDocumentAsync<T>(Document doc, string name, Func<RevitTransactionContext, T> action, CancellationToken ct = default); } Delegates receive RevitTransactionContext, which carries the UIApplication and the Document. TransactionRunner runs on IRevitCallGate and applies the synchronous delegate admission before it enters the gate or starts a transaction. The runtime awaitable check for a reference-typed result runs inside the transaction body, so an awaitable result rolls the transaction back before commit. If doc.IsModifiable (a transaction is already open), it uses a SubTransaction; otherwise it starts a Transaction. It refuses to start a transaction on one document while another document is modifiable. It attaches TransactionFailurePreprocessor, which suppresses non-critical Revit warnings. await _transactionRunner.RunInActiveDocumentAsync("Create Wall", context => { Wall.Create(context.Document, curve, levelId, false); }); var wallId = await _transactionRunner.RunInActiveDocumentAsync("Create Wall", context => Wall.Create(context.Document, curve, levelId, false).Id); Failure handling TransactionFailurePreprocessor.AttachToTransaction sets clear-after-rollback before failure processing starts. A warning is reported as suppressed only after Revit deletes it. A blocking failure, or a fault in a failure accessor, records a blocking diagnostic and requests rollback. An accessor fault keeps the caught exception, which becomes the InnerException of the TransactionFailureException (an AggregateException when several accessors failed). An attachment fault propagates before commit; the preprocessor does not change rollback options inside the failure callback. The preprocessor keeps one TransactionFailureRecord per message it reads: severity, description, failure definition GUID, failing element IDs and whether the message rolled the transaction back. A fault while reading the failing element IDs is added to AccessorFaults and does not change how the message resolves. A runner built with new TransactionRunner(gate, logger) logs every record and every accessor fault at Warning after the commit; the one-argument constructor logs nothing. GM's apply runners use the logging form. TransactionFailureException is the public diagnostic for a transaction that did not reach Committed. Its constructors are internal to Core. Callers read the transaction name, final status, warnings, blocking failure text and failure-definition identities from its properties. A posted blocking failure rolls back a runner-managed transaction and raises this exception with the transaction name and the blocking diagnostic. Tool write boundaries map this exception and Revit refusal exceptions to their own typed failures and keep the original exception as the inner cause. Sources: src/DBTools.Core/Revit/Transactions/{TransactionRunner,TransactionExecutor,TransactionBoundary,TransactionFailurePreprocessor}.cs. Transaction groups ITransactionGroupService makes several transactions on the active document one Revit undo entry. It is the manual lifecycle; the caller owns the try/finally around FinalizeAsync, in the workflow that knows whether to commit or roll back. public interface ITransactionGroupService { bool IsActive { get; } Task BeginAsync(string name, CancellationToken ct = default); Task FinalizeAsync(TransactionGroupFinalization finalization, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<bool> IsGroupHealthyAsync(CancellationToken ct = default); } If the document is already modifiable, BeginAsync creates no group, IsActive becomes true, and FinalizeAsync only resets state. FinalizeAsync accepts only TransactionGroupFinalization.Commit (assimilate) and Rollback; another value fails before the inactive-session check. Finalization always clears the active group state and attempts disposal of the owned group. If the operation and the cleanup both fail, the operation failure comes first in an ordered aggregate. Revit rolls back a group that is still open when the API callback that started it returns, and RevitTransactionGroups.Begin ends the queued turn after the current call. Separate BeginAsync and FinalizeAsync calls therefore keep one group only on an InlineUi gate inside one callback, as the modal SGT and TDV commands use them. Queued modeless work uses IAtomicTransactionGroup.RunAsync(name, work, keep, ct), which TransactionGroupService also implements; GM commit review constructs it directly for its gate. In one gate call it begins the group, runs the work, then assimilates the group when keep(result) is true and rolls it back otherwise. The group is one Revit undo entry also under the queued gate. An exception, or a cancellation seen at any point before finalization (also after the work returns), rolls the group back and propagates. A document that already has an open transaction is refused before any work, because the group would own nothing to roll back. The work must complete inside the callback, where its gate calls run inline. Work still pending when the callback returns is canceled and the group is rolled back. The outcome is classified by the group status Revit reports: only RolledBack counts as discarded and only Committed as kept. Any other status throws TransactionGroupOutcomeUnknownException, and the caller must not report the work as discarded. Progress overlay Hosts Host tool views through ToolWindowFactory and IToolWindowSession. The modal and modeless shells expose the WPF owner. Core installs WindowInitializer before the XAML loads and retires its state with the session. Bind an overlay to its window with ProgressOverlay.For(window, logger), on the owner's UI thread. State, dispatcher affinity and diagnostics stay tied to that window. The logger is required. ProgressOverlayWindowCapability (ProgressOverlayWindowCapability.Hosts.cs) is the only registry from Window to overlay state and visual host. There is no ambient or process-global host. ProgressOverlay.Operations.cs holds the public lifecycle API. ProgressOverlayRunWorkflow.cs owns RunAsync(...): the show policy, the linked cancellation source, cancel observation and hide sequencing. ProgressOverlayDelayedHideScheduler keeps the dispatcher operation it posts and observes every outcome. It clears the pending hide only when the completing operation owns the current cancellation source, so an aborted or faulted stale operation cannot clear a replacement hide. IProgressOverlay Member Behavior Show(title, cancelable) Shows the overlay and resets the cancellation state. Update(status, progress01) Sets status text and progress in [0,1]. A null argument leaves that value unchanged. A non-finite progress value throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException before status or progress changes. Finite values are clamped to [0,1]. UpdateStep(current, total, description, progress01) Sets the status to Step X/Y: {description}. Scope(title, cancelable) Returns a disposable scope. Nested scopes restore the parent state in LIFO order. CancelRequested Thread-safe snapshot of the Cancel button state. RequestCancel() Sets CancelRequested.
