Hide() Hides the overlay and clears transient state. RunAsync(title, work, cancelable, options, ct) Runs work with an overlay lifecycle and cancellation bridge. A second run on the same window while one is active throws InvalidOperationException. ProgressOverlay marshals public calls to its owner's WPF dispatcher. Do not change overlay state directly from a background thread. Pure and view-model tests can use a simple IProgressOverlay double. Rendering A status change forces a render (RequestRender(force: true)); a progress-only update is throttled. Phase changes stay visible when Revit starves the dispatcher. ProgressOverlayRenderScheduler throttles render requests to one per 30 ms and pumps one dispatcher frame (DispatcherFramePump.TryPumpSingleFrame) with a 20 ms budget and a depth guard. A forced render bypasses the pending-render guard. A pending render older than 250 ms is treated as stuck and replaced. Do not add other dispatcher pump loops or dispatcher-frame code outside that helper while Revit work is active. Cancellation Use RunAsync(...) for long operations. ProgressOverlayRunWorkflow observes CancelRequested, cancels a linked token source and passes the work delegate a token that fires on cancel. After Show(...) resets the cancellation state, the cancel watcher starts before the work begins. SGT analysis (AnalysisSessionWorkflow), SGT placement (PlacementWorkflow) and GM commit review (CommitReviewApplyOverlayWorkflow) use RunAsync. A workflow that drives its own Scope(...) reads CancelRequested and bridges it to its own cancellation. TDV transfer does this: its reporter returns Overlay.CancelRequested as IsCancellationRequested. using (Overlay.Scope("Transferring Drafting Views", cancelable: true)) { result = await _session.ApplySelectionAsync(items, reporter, CancellationToken.None); } Progress values Tools report IProgress<(string message, double? progress01)>: a status message and an optional fraction in [0,1]. MonotonicProgressAdapter (src/DBTools.Core/Progress/Aggregation) wraps such a reporter and forwards non-decreasing values clamped to [0,1]. A null fraction forwards the status and does not change the tracked value. A non-finite fraction throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException and does not change the tracked value. Create one adapter per operation. Tool Progress source Overlay mapping GM MappingPlanExecutor reports per-writer progress (writerIndex / writerCount); MappingApplyState.ReportProgress(message, progress01) reports within a writer. CommitReviewApplyWorkflow wraps the reporter in MonotonicProgressAdapter; CommitReviewApplyOverlayWorkflow updates the overlay. TDV The transfer executor reports per-view stage percentages (0, 10, 25, 35, 60, 85, 100). TdvWindowViewModel.UpdateTransferOverlayProgress maps them through six weighted stages and never decreases. SGT PlacementExecutor.PlaceAsync / UpdateAsync report wall-level and sub-step progress. PlacementWorkflow wraps the overlay in MonotonicProgressAdapter. Record Set ExecutionPlanExecutor.ExecuteAsync takes an Action<int> percentage and an Action<string> log. PlanExecutionWorkflow combines the last percentage with each log message in one overlay update. Common failures Dispatcher errors or missing state: an overlay call on a window that Core WindowInitializer did not initialize, or a change that bypasses the overlay API. Invalid Revit API context: Revit API calls outside IRevitCallGate, or async delegates inside the gate.

developer-guide/architecture/sandbox-val.title: Sandbox Validator | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/sandbox-val.summary: Sandbox Validator DBTools.Sandbox validates one staged product year without Revit. In headless mode it checks the candidate files, metadata and manifests. On Windows it also builds the real tool windows and checks themes, layout, bindings and Dispatcher cleanup. It is also a host for developing tool UI with design-time view models. Synopsis DBTools.Sandbox [--headless] [--dist-dir DIR] [--revit-reference-dir DIR] Option Description --headless Run static and metadata validation without creating windows. Requires --revit-reference-dir. --dist-dir DIR A year directory (for example .artifacts/dist/Release/2026) or a distribution root that contains year directories. Default: .artifacts/dist/Release of the repository that contains the executable, else of the current directory. --revit-reference-dir DIR Revit reference metadata for the year, checked against the installed runtime. Valid only with --headless. Both --option VALUE and --option=VALUE are accepted. An empty value, an unknown argument or a missing value is an error. Without --headless, Sandbox runs interactively against the installed Revit runtime. WSL paths of the form /mnt/<drive>/... are converted to Windows paths. Example, after ./build.sh BuildAll: dotnet run --project src/DBTools.Sandbox/DBTools.Sandbox.csproj -- \ --headless --dist-dir .artifacts/dist/Release/2026 \ --revit-reference-dir /path/to/Revit2026 The exit status is 1 when validation fails before WPF starts; the error is written to standard error. Process model Each year runs in a new process in the default load context: SandboxEntry uses only BCL types. It parses the options, resolves the year directory and runs SandboxCandidate.Validate. A non-inlined method prepares the Revit runtime resolver and loads HandyControl, Presentation, Core, App and the manifest-declared tools from their candidate paths. A second non-inlined method starts the WPF application. The JIT compiles this call only after the candidate assemblies are loaded, so Core and WPF cannot resolve from anywhere else first. The process exits after validation, so no assembly of one candidate stays loaded for another year. Sandbox creates no load context, does not run App's Revit startup, does not load Revit reference files as product assemblies and does not probe subfolders other than Tools/. Candidate contract A candidate is one year directory of the product tree. SandboxCandidate checks the add-in file, the top-level files, the flat Tools/ directory, the PE simple names, and conflicts with assemblies already loaded in the process. No third-party DLL may be present. Validation sequence Resolve the year directory and the optional Revit reference directory. Check DBTools.addin, the exact top-level files, the recursive Tools/ files, the supported year and framework, and the PE simple names. Read the App, Core, Presentation, HandyControl and tool references and their source-derived versions from PE metadata, without loading Revit API assemblies. Discover the embedded manifests and validate module, command, availability, icon, raw XAML and design-time view model ownership. On Windows (not --headless), load the resources and themes, build each window, run layout and interaction checks, capture binding errors, close every window and verify Dispatcher cleanup. Portable validation of a distribution archive checks the same file set and also file lengths and SHA-256 hashes. Components Component Responsibility SandboxEntry BCL-only option parsing, year selection, candidate check and the non-inlined WPF start SandboxCandidate Candidate files, direct image loading, PE identity and loaded-image path checks SandboxDistributionContext References to the candidate's App, Core, Presentation, HandyControl and tool assemblies and manifests ManifestValidator Manifest owners, commands, availability types, raw resources and design-time view models AssemblyMetadataInspector PE metadata and reference identities, read from bytes without running Revit code HeadlessValidationWorkflow The headless sequence and its structured result ToolWindowValidator Window construction, layout, interaction, binding errors and cleanup The portable manifest rules are in testing/DBTools.Distribution.Validation/Manifest/PortableToolManifestValidator.cs. Tool window registration A tool lists its Sandbox windows in manifest.yml: sandboxWindows: - id: DBTools.MyTool.Main displayName: "My Tool" group: "Common" xamlResource: "DBTools.ToolViews.MyTool.MyToolView.xaml" windowKind: Modal designTimeViewModelType: "DBTools.MyTool.App.DesignTime.MyToolDesignTimeViewModel" designTimeViewModelAssembly: "DBTools.MyTool" designTimeViewModelVisibility: Public windowKind is Modal or Modeless. SandboxCatalog (Core) reads these entries into window specifications, and Sandbox hosts each raw view in the stable Presentation ToolWindowHost. No candidate Window type crosses between assemblies. Validation requires, for each entry: a nonempty id, displayName, group, xamlResource, designTimeViewModelType and designTimeViewModelAssembly; an EmbeddedResource in the owning project with exactly that LogicalName; a root element that derives from FrameworkElement and is not a Window; the host supplies the window shell; no x:Class, x:ClassModifier or x:FieldModifier, no code-behind event attributes, no CLR namespaces of the tool assembly, no implicit templates for tool types, no inferred DataGrid columns and no pack URIs into the tool assembly; a concrete design-time view model whose visibility matches designTimeViewModelVisibility (Public or Internal) and that has a parameterless constructor (public for Public); Sandbox invokes it. Give it fixed display data and no Revit, network or settings services. Tool code can check DBTools.Core.Sandbox.SandboxMode.IsActive to avoid services that do not exist in Sandbox. Every manifest command type must implement IExternalCommand and every availability type IExternalCommandAvailability, in the declared owner assembly under Tools/. Window checks ToolWindowValidator opens each raw view through ToolWindowHost with its design-time view model and then: measures and arranges the window at a fixed size and at infinite size; selects every tab of each TabControl and restores the original tab; shows the row details of the first three rows of each nonempty DataGrid, except grids whose details are VisibleWhenSelected; records WPF binding errors; closes the window and waits for a bounded ApplicationIdle Dispatcher barrier. It fails when the Dispatcher is missing, shutting down or aborted, or when a cleanup operation is still pending after the barrier. Build output and archives Sandbox is built once per year, although both years use the same framework: .artifacts/sandbox/<Configuration>/<year>/<TFM>/ build output sandbox/<year>/<sanitized-tfm>/ path inside the validation archive ./build.sh PackageSandboxValidationInput writes a content-addressed validate-dist-<sha256>.zip with the candidate and Sandbox. The DIST suite consumes that archive and writes a structured result JSON (see Distribution acceptance). The archive and the result keep normalized relative paths. A headless or Linux run checks files and metadata only; the window checks run only on Windows. Troubleshooting Failure Where to look Candidate file missing or extra ProductOutput staging and DistributionContract .addin entry mismatch build/Installer/DBTools.addin and the App output Tool assembly missing The manifest assembly name and Tools/ staging Raw XAML resource missing EmbeddedResource LogicalName in the owning project Design-time view model cannot be created Its visibility, designTimeViewModelVisibility and parameterless constructor Binding errors Explicit bindings and the stable Presentation templates Layout failure ToolWindowValidator measure and arrange messages Cleanup timeout Dispatcher and window owner lifetime A window failure reports both the primary exception and any cleanup exception. See Sandbox Integration, Assembly Loading Contract and Test Pipeline.

developer-guide/architecture/structural-.title: Structural Preview | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/structural-.summary: Structural Preview DBTools.Presentation.StructuralPreview is the stable WPF host for the structural 3D preview shared by ERFT and SGT. A tool adapter supplies immutable scene data and receives pointer events. The host owns the Helix viewport, effects manager, camera, navigation, materials, hit testing, tooltip, overlay markers and cleanup. Helix and SharpDX are merged into Presentation as internal types; no tool assembly or raw view names them. ERFT and SGT register the presenter's disposal with their tool-window sessions. The component has no Core, App or tool-assembly dependency. Its public scene records contain only immutable arrays, System.Numerics values, strings, integers and scalar values. Attach and dispose Call StructuralPreview3DFactory.Attach on the viewport host dispatcher. The ContentControl must be empty. The optional overlay canvas must use the same dispatcher. The returned IStructuralPreview3D owns one viewport and one effects manager. All presenter methods and disposal are synchronous UI-thread operations. Attach returns a disabled presenter without loading or creating Helix objects when StructuralPreview3DOptions.Disabled is true, and returns one with the load error as its reason when the Helix libraries cannot be loaded. The disabled presenter still validates and copies supplied scene and emphasis data, reports its status reason, returns false from projection, and can be disposed repeatedly. For an available presenter, Dispose removes viewport, camera, owner-window, timer and input handlers; closes the tooltip; removes only the overlay children created by this presenter; disposes owned scene elements, viewport and effects manager; clears scene data and subscriber events; and clears the host content only when that content is still the viewport owned by this presenter. Cleanup is synchronous and does not post a dispatcher frame. Disposal clears subscriptions before cleanup, so it publishes zero presenter events during or after disposal. Repeated disposal is safe. Scene data and picks SetScene validates and deep-copies the supplied records and arrays. The caller may then release or reuse its own objects. Equal mesh geometry keeps existing Helix models; geometry or appearance changes update the rendered decorations and materials, while bounds or exterior-normal changes update camera state. Mesh Opacity supplies the material alpha and overrides the alpha byte in Argb. Line sets multiply their ARGB alpha by Opacity. Selection and hover colors preserve the mesh opacity. Mesh picking is independent of emphasis. A mesh is eligible for a hit only when its supplied IsPickable value is true; context meshes can therefore be pickable or non-pickable independently of their material role. A floor is supplied as scene geometry, normally a context mesh with IsPickable: false. Line sets and non-pickable meshes do not produce mesh hits. A missed hit has null mesh ID, null context ID and null world point. A hit's mesh and context hits are resolved independently: each is the nearest eligible hit for its role. MeshId is the nearest member ID, or null when there is no member hit; ContextId is the nearest context ID independently. WorldPoint is the nearest member hit point when one exists, otherwise the context hit point, so a context-only hit has a null mesh ID and a context world point. The event also carries WPF screen coordinates relative to the viewport and keyboard modifiers. SetEmphasis accepts one emphasis state per mesh ID. The presenter applies selection, segment-selection, sibling, dimmed and hover material policies from the selected StructuralPreviewPalette. StructuralPreviewPalette.Sgt and .Erft are the adapter presets. They differ in member color boost, surfaces, selection and hover colors, and edge and outline settings, and use the same renderer. The presenter adds a pivot marker to the supplied overlay canvas while orbiting. The marker and all generated WPF objects have their data context cleared or blocked so tool data contexts do not flow into the stable visual tree. Home views and camera movement The ExteriorThreeQuarter strategy is the SGT home view. When bounds or the exterior normal changes, the session recomputes and stores a raw Home camera. Its exact formula is: distance = max(2.2 * boundsDiagonal, 8) yaw = 28 degrees pitch = 0.22 downward along the configured up axis The exterior normal is projected onto the up plane. A missing horizontal normal uses negative Y as the stable fallback. The stored Home keeps this exact distance. Clamping applies to the displayed camera only. If the user has moved the camera, a changed scene clamps the current camera and retains the new raw Home for a later reset. Reset clears the moved flag, applies Home, and clamps the displayed camera. ERFT uses the PreserveAngle strategy. When bounds change, the session fits the current view angle and captures that result as Home. The fit formula is: halfV = radians(fieldOfView) / 2 halfH = atan(tan(halfV) * aspect) distance = max(boundsDiagonal / 2 / sin(min(halfV, halfH)), 2) * 1.2 Helix FieldOfView is the vertical angle. The fit keeps the bounds' bounding sphere inside both the vertical and the horizontal field of view, so the whole scene is visible at the viewport aspect when the fit runs; the distance clamp still applies. Scene constraints use these bounds-only constants (StructuralPreviewCameraMath): diagonal = actualDiagonal, or 10 when actualDiagonal <= 1e-6 min = clamp(diagonal * 0.0005, 0.005, 0.75) max = clamp(diagonal * 40, min * 2, 50000) targetPad = max(2, diagonal * 6) near = max(0.0005, min * 0.05) far = max(100, max * 2) When a scene changes mesh geometry without changing these bounds, the presenter keeps the stored Home object and only updates its owned render models. Adapters must compute bounds from every mesh vertex so a real extent change is reported as a bounds change; a bounds change is an intentional Home refit under PreserveAngle. ZoomToFit performs the exact fit. When FitRedefinesHome is enabled, the fitted camera becomes Home and the viewport default camera is updated to the same pose; otherwise the fit marks the camera as user-moved while preserving Home. ResetView restores stored Home. Pan uses screen-space camera axes, orbit uses the configured arbitrary up axis around the selected or picked pivot, and wheel zoom moves toward the picked world anchor. Gesture cancellation occurs on lost capture, window deactivation, unload and disabled interaction. The viewport's native view cube handles its own preview input before scene picking. The presenter keeps the default camera synchronized with stored scene Home when a scene is attached; an explicit fit also updates it when FitRedefinesHome is enabled. Input and hover StructuralPreview3DOptions.ShowTooltips defaults to true. It enables the stable presenter's mesh tooltips. When disabled, pointer updates keep the tooltip closed. Materials and lighting Adapters choose StructuralPreviewPalette.Sgt or .Erft and can copy the record to adjust individual values. A palette supplies member and context surfaces, key/fill/rim/ambient light colors, sibling and dimmed policies, selection and hover colors, emissive scaling, edge colors and thickness, outline mode and pivot colors. IsPickable controls hit testing. A non-pickable context mesh remains rendered with its base context material but bypasses selection, segment-selection, sibling, dimmed and hover emphasis; pickable context meshes can receive context hover, sibling and dimmed states but never member selection states. The SGT preset uses these alpha rules. Sibling emphasis scales diffuse alpha by 0.70 and retains the source ambient, specular and emissive alpha. Dimmed emphasis sets every channel's alpha to max(0.05, sourceAlpha * 0.45). Hovering a sibling restores the base material and adds emissive brightness while preserving its source alpha. Hovering a dimmed mesh adds emissive brightness and retains the dimmed alpha. The default options select the SGT palette and exterior home strategy. ERFT selects both its palette and its camera strategy: var options = new StructuralPreview3DOptions { Palette = StructuralPreviewPalette.Erft, HomeView = StructuralPreviewHomeView.PreserveAngle }; Diagnostics and projection Diagnostic reports debug, warning and error messages as plain strings with an optional exception. Repeated identical diagnostic messages are suppressed for two seconds. An initialization or disabled-path diagnostic is delivered once to the first diagnostic subscriber; the reason is also available in Status. Event publication takes an invocation-list snapshot and stops when a callback disposes the presenter. No presenter event is raised after Dispose clears subscriptions. On the first render failure, the presenter changes to Unavailable, disables interaction, cancels navigation, clears hover state, stops its clamp timer and collapses the viewport. It reports that failure as an error diagnostic, subject to the two-second diagnostic de-duplication; later render failures are ignored while the presenter is unavailable. TryProjectToViewport returns false when the presenter is unavailable, disposed, unloaded, has no render context, receives a non-finite point, has an invalid camera or the point is behind the camera. It returns WPF device- independent coordinates relative to the viewport on success. Projection failures are reported as debug diagnostics and never escape as exceptions. developer-guide/architecture/test-pipeli.title: Test Pipeline | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/test-pipeli.summary: Test Pipeline This page describes how DB Tools tests are selected, staged and run. For the test.sh options, examples and the rules for writing tests, see Testing Tools. DB Tools tests run through one of two routes: ./test.sh resolves the selected projects, builds them, freezes their inputs and runs them locally or submits them to the dbtools-daemon fleet. It writes the receipts that --no-build and CI consume. See the test.sh command reference. Plain dotnet test on an entry project in testing/Daemon/ uses the pinned daemon VSTest adapter (DbToolsDaemon.RevitTest.TestAdapter). MSBuild builds the selected assemblies, models, includes and per-year sources, and the adapter submits them in one request. See Daemon adapter entry projects. Use one route per invocation. Both read the relay URL from DBTOOLS_DAEMON_RELAY_URL; the daemon owns relay credentials, and neither route accepts or stores them. Scopes and suites Scope or suite Marker Where it runs Pure tests (pure) plain [Test] Without Revit. Locally when possible; otherwise as a daemon PureSuite job on a hidden Windows desktop Revit-hosted tests (local) [RevitLocal] Inside Revit on a daemon worker, for one selected year Design Automation tests (da) [RevitDA] On the invoking host, as an HTTP client of APS Design Automation; never through the daemon DIST The Windows distribution acceptance suite, always a daemon PureSuite job BUILD Linux-native build and distribution contract suites Revit-hosted tests exercise the real ribbon, WPF and add-in lifecycle in Revit. Design Automation tests build the Revit 2026 Sentinel WorkItem test project and run it with dotnet test; see APS Design Automation Sentinel. Pure requests have no year. A Revit-hosted request for two years makes one daemon request per year, each with its own product tree and report. Design Automation tests always build Revit 2026. Selection test.sh list --projects prints the sorted scope<TAB>project rows and is the source of truth for what a request selects. It evaluates project membership, explicit Compile Include, Exclude and Remove items, disabled default items, NUnit fixture attributes and the selected tool, scope and year. The same index resolves fixtures and exact FQNs. A fixture must resolve to one compiled owner class. An unknown fixture or project, an unreadable project or source file, a project the selected tool and scope cannot reach, or an explicit scope with no resolved project exits with status 2 before any build or submission. An exact FullyQualifiedName=<FQN> filter becomes an exact daemon selector, and a prefix filter becomes a prefix selector. A Revit-hosted filter that cannot be mapped exits with status 2 instead of selecting the whole assembly. Pure routing test.sh checks each selected Pure assembly for its .deps.json, .runtimeconfig.json and the output-local NUnit3.TestAdapter.dll, then routes it: to the daemon if it is the DIST suite or a machine is pinned; to the daemon if it targets Windows and the host is not Windows; to the daemon if the host lacks Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App; a missing other framework is an error; otherwise to local VSTest. Projects that run locally, including the Linux BUILD and Distribution suites, run one after another; daemon submissions run concurrently, at most DBT_PURE_CONCURRENCY (default 2) at a time. A local project that runs zero tests fails. With a filter expression, the run fails only when no selected project runs a test. Linux-native BUILD projects and *.Portable.Pure.Tests projects are skipped on Windows with a notice. Inputs and receipts For a selected scope and year, the MSBuild graph returns the test assembly, target framework, model items and product-tree includes in one pass. Before any submission, test.sh freezes the assemblies, runtime closure, product-tree includes, models and companions into the content-addressed test input cache (DBT_TEST_INPUT_CACHE_ROOT), so a later build cannot change the submitted files. A normal exit removes the per-run directory. --compile-only writes a receipt bound to the source identity, the selected projects, the graph inputs and the output hashes. --no-build verifies all of these and refuses stale or missing files. CI resolves the selectors once with ./test.sh list --projects, compiles each selected scope with --compile-only, transfers the receipt and the recorded input closure, and runs them with --no-build. The consumer never rebuilds. Linux BUILD and DIST jobs do not depend on the Windows transfer. The build and distribution suites read already-built product metadata and reject a stale source snapshot. Source, build and test changes alter the snapshot; documentation and transient artifacts do not. Results The daemon terminal JSON is the result. A successful run must report a positive executed count; a report of zero tests fails. A distinctive nonzero daemon exit status is kept even when the terminal JSON is missing or malformed. Independent scopes in one request continue after a failure, but test.sh returns the first nonzero status and never reports a failed run as passed. Daemon adapter entry projects testing/Daemon/Hosted/<Tool>.Hosted.Entry.csproj builds the Revit-hosted tests of that owner for both years (Hosted2026.proj, Hosted2027.proj). testing/Daemon/Pure/<Tool>.Pure.Entry.csproj selects every DBTools.<Tool>.*Pure.Tests.csproj beside its owner. After the build, the entry writes dbtools-daemon.runsettings from Hosted.runsettings or Pure.runsettings with the literal sources, models and includes. The hosted settings default to years 2026,2027, isolated execution and a 30-minute timeout, and treat a run with no tests as an error. Product staging Each Revit-hosted test for a year receives the product tree that the installer uses, under product/<year>/. The tree keeps its relative paths. Test assemblies and NUnit and adapter dependencies are separate inputs. App loads tools from Tools/ by explicit path into the context that holds it, so ProductLoadContext and DevModeLoadContext receive the same identities as the staged tree. Test support installs no resolver for product assemblies. Test projects Test projects are next to their production owners: src/DBTools.App/Tests/DBTools.App.{Pure,Local}.Tests.csproj src/DBTools.Core/Tests/DBTools.Core.{Pure,Local}.Tests.csproj src/DBTools.Sandbox/Tests/DBTools.Sandbox.Pure.Tests.csproj src/Tools/<Category>/<Tool>/Tests/DBTools.<Tool>.{Pure,Local}.Tests.csproj testing/DBTools.Build.Tests/ build and distribution contracts (Linux) testing/DBTools.Distribution.Tests/ portable archive contracts (Linux) testing/DBTools.Distribution.Windows.Tests/ DIST suite testing/RevitTestModels/ test models by year and tool An owner has both a .Pure.Tests and a .Local.Tests project only when both kinds of test exist. Pure projects list their source files explicitly and reference their normal production owners. Shared props give every Pure project $(DBT_PureRevitYear) (2026) and static graph restore, and pass that year on owner references, so a plain dotnet build or dotnet test of one project needs no properties. Revit is compile-only in Pure tests: a test must not load Revit-typed members or scan owner types outside the loadable set. .Local.Tests projects disable default compile items and include only Revit-hosted fixtures. Presentation behavior tests are under Presentation; the Core Pure projects link the fixtures they can run without Revit. Tests that need a real WPF window run where Windows is available. Portable Pure projects Core and SGT define an optional $(DBT_PortableTargetFramework). Their *.Portable.Pure.Tests projects build against that framework and run on Linux; CI and Windows test.sh route them to Linux. To make a project portable: declare desktop and portable TargetFrameworks; condition DBT_RevitHostIdentity, UseWPF and the Presentation ProjectReference on the desktop framework, and keep Revit references under the desktop host identity condition; set DBT_UsesMergedAssemblies=false in portable consumers. build/MSBuild/Portable.targets excludes App, Revit, Views, DesignTime and XAML inputs. Portable images use ordinary NuGet dependencies, have no content version and add no staged runtime files. Core uses an explicit list of source files for its portable build. Test models Revit-hosted projects declare RevitTestModel items relative to testing/RevitTestModels: testing/RevitTestModels/ ├── 2026/GM/gm_test_model.rvt ├── 2026/SGT/sgt_test_model.rvt ├── 2026/SGT/_LinkedModels/sgt_test_linked_model.rvt ├── 2026/Regression/realtest_model.rvt ├── 2027/... (same layout) ├── GM/SharedParameters/shared_parameters.txt └── VTC/vtc_import_layers.dxf Model files and explicit non-RVT inputs keep their relative paths in the daemon stage. Revit-hosted fixtures find them under DBTOOLS_DAEMON_REVIT_MODELS_DIR; Pure fixtures use the repository root in DBT_TEST_REPO_ROOT. TestPathResolver reads the root on every call, so a job never sees the model root of a previous job. A fixture may open a temporary copy of a model, but the daemon owns the active document and the worker lifecycle. Models resolve only from these roots, not from a worker checkout or an %APPDATA% cache. Test support testing/TestSupport holds shared test infrastructure and doubles for true externals. Tool-specific doubles are under testing/TestSupport/<Tool> and are linked as source by the matching test projects; they are not a separate assembly. Revit/RevitHost.cs initializes the year, the App runtime and the product Revit call gate before the test body, and supplies the real UIApplication through an ambient scope that does not carry API access across an await. It owns the scheduler unless a fixture holds a longer lease. Forced-queue tests call the real external-event handler synchronously to model a later API turn; one daemon NUnit callback contains no second native turn. Wpf/WpfTestRuntimeBootstrap.cs registers pack URI support, installs the shared window owner, validates themes in the runtime assembly's contextual reflection scope, and releases only its own provider at teardown. It adds no Resolving handlers and does not force Presentation or HandyControl into the default context. Logging/TestLoggingBridge.cs uses production logging when Revit provides it and a console and file host otherwise. Revit-hosted fixtures release only their own runtime, Revit task, owner handle and window resources. Cleanup reports both the primary failure and any cleanup failure. See Build Pipeline, Assembly Loading Contract and Sandbox Validator.

developer-guide/architecture/theme-syste.title: Theme System | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/theme-syste.summary: Theme System DBTools.Presentation.dll holds every compiled WPF resource of the product: the theme dictionaries, stable controls and window shells. It stays loaded for the life of the Revit process. Tool views are raw XAML that Presentation parses at run time, so App, Core and the tool assemblies contain no BAML and no .g.resources. Each window merges the theme into its own resources, never into Application.Resources, so DB Tools does not change the appearance of other add-ins. Assembly roles Assembly Compiled WPF content DBTools.Presentation Theme dictionaries, stable windows and controls, tool behaviors and converters under Tools/<TOOL>/, the merged Helix theme, and the settings views of DialogSuppression, ElevationTags, FoundationTags and JoistGirderWeight (linked from those tool folders) DBTools.HandyControl The HandyControl skins and themes DBTools.Core None. Window lifecycle, error boundaries, registry, commands and runtime hosts can be reloaded Tool assemblies None. Tool views are embedded as raw XAML Presentation keeps explicit Page, Compile and EmbeddedResource items (EnableDefaultPageItems=false). The linked tool settings views keep their tool namespaces, for example DBTools.DialogSuppression.Settings.Views; the tool projects remove them from their own Page items. Tool views A tool embeds each view as an EmbeddedResource with the logical name DBTools.ToolViews.<TOOL>.<View>.xaml. ToolWindowFactory.Create (Core) opens a view in these steps: ToolWindowHost.Create (Presentation) creates a stable shell, ToolWindowModalShell or ToolWindowModelessShell. The shell initializer runs before the view is parsed. The default is WindowInitializer.Initialize or InitializeModeless, which applies the theme, binds the owner window, registers the progress overlay and installs the error boundary and logging. ToolWindowXaml.LoadElement parses the raw view inside ToolWindowReflectionScope, and the view and shell receive the tool's view model as DataContext. The factory registers the session in ToolWindowRegistry. The caller shows the window with session.ShowDialog() or session.Show() and gets named controls with session.Require<T>(name). The Settings, Alert, Logger and notification banner windows are raw resources in Presentation and use the same loader; so do tool template dictionaries such as the VTC diff templates and the SGT opening view. For these windows Core keeps the state, commands and lifecycle and event handling; the controls need no typed constructor from a reloadable assembly and do no type discovery at run time. Retirement tears down bindings, automation roots, resources and callbacks. Core lifecycle handlers are released through BehaviorState and session cleanup before the shell closes. A custom shell initializer releases its own handles. Raw views name only framework types or public stable Presentation types and merge the theme through Presentation's ResourceUri markup extension before they use static theme keys. Tool content uses explicit keyed templates. SGT's opening and girt grids use stable behaviors over tool row state. ERFT and SGT pass immutable scene data to the stable 3D viewport, which owns camera, material, picking and device state (see Structural Preview). Theme dictionaries The root dictionary is: /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Theme.xaml <PresentationVersion> is the content version of the Presentation assembly (see Build Pipeline). The root merges, in this order: /DBTools.HandyControl;V<HandyControlVersion>;component/Themes/SkinDark.xaml /DBTools.HandyControl;V<HandyControlVersion>;component/Themes/Theme.xaml /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Tokens.xaml /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Brushes.xaml /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Converters.xaml /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Controls.xaml /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/DataGrid.xaml /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Menus.xaml /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Components.xaml ThemeResourceLoader (Core) checks this order. At startup ThemeValidator.ValidateOrThrow registers the pack URI scheme, loads each dictionary separately and freezes its freezables, loads the root and checks its merged dictionaries, and then measures and arranges a probe tree of standard controls. A failure stops startup; see Troubleshooting. Resource URIs Every compiled resource URI contains the assembly's version. A changed stable assembly therefore has a new identity, and WPF cannot select an older copy of Presentation or HandyControl that an earlier DB Tools version has already loaded. Presentation URIs use the Presentation version, and HandyControl URIs use the HandyControl version. The component URI is relative, so Application.LoadComponent does not need the pack scheme to be registered. Use ResourceUri.CreateResourceUri for Application.LoadComponent, dictionary sources and the dictionary markup extensions. Use ResourceUri.CreateAbsoluteResourceUri for images and icons created in code without a WPF base URI. It registers the pack scheme and returns pack://application:,,,/<assembly>;V<version>;component/<path>. WindowInitializer loads the window icon with BitmapCacheOption.OnLoad inside its warning boundary; otherwise WPF can defer the file lookup until it creates the window handle. XAML namespaces XAML outside Presentation refers to stable types with clr-namespace:...;assembly=DBTools.Presentation. XAML compiled by Presentation uses the namespace form without assembly=. This keeps the BAML compiler from resolving Presentation types through a reloadable assembly. BAML assembly versions The BAML assembly table must contain the final assembly version, because WPF resolves local markup extensions through that table separately from the outer pack URI. Keep SDK assembly-info generation on in WPF temporary projects. With it off, BAML references Version=0.0.0.0; if an older Presentation is already loaded in the default context, the CLR can satisfy that request with the older copy. That copy lacks HandyControlResourceUriExtension, and WPF throws NotImplementedException before it opens the HandyControl dictionaries. WPF's local-assembly fallback runs only when loading throws, so a successful bind to the older copy bypasses it. See .NET 10 WPF assembly and type resolution and CoreCLR version compatibility. developer-guide/architecture/wiki-server.title: Wiki Server | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/wiki-server.summary: Wiki Server wiki/server-config/ holds the configuration of the web server that serves this documentation site at https://dbtools.greatwhitelab.net. The server runs Caddy for the static files and a webhook container that updates them. A push to the main branch of the kirsch33/dbtools-wiki repository makes the server pull the new site. Publishing flow The Documentation workflow (.github/workflows/documentation.yml, manual dispatch) builds the site with .github/scripts/build-docs.sh and pushes wiki/_site to the main branch of kirsch33/dbtools-wiki. It authenticates with the deploy key in the WIKI_DEPLOY_KEY secret. GitHub sends the push event of kirsch33/dbtools-wiki to https://dbtools.greatwhitelab.net/hooks/dbtools-wiki, signed with the shared secret in the X-Hub-Signature-256 header. Caddy proxies /hooks/* to the webhook container on port 9000. The dbtools-wiki hook runs only when the HMAC-SHA256 signature is valid, repository.full_name is kirsch33/dbtools-wiki and ref is refs/heads/main. It then runs /scripts/pull-site.sh dbtools-wiki. pull-site.sh reads the site entry from sites.json. On first use it clones the branch with depth 1 into the web directory; after that it fetches the branch and runs git reset --hard origin/<branch>. Caddy serves /web/dbtools-wiki as static files. A path that matches no file or directory returns /index.html. Files File Content Dockerfile The webhook image: almir/webhook, pinned by digest, plus bash, git and jq. It runs as the base image's unprivileged webhook user. docker-compose.yml The webhook service: builds the image, runs webhook -verbose -template -hooks=/etc/webhook/hooks.json -hotreload, mounts config/ and scripts/ read-only and /web read-write, reads webhook.env, and joins the external caddy_default network. webhook.env.example Template for webhook.env, which sets WEBHOOK_SECRET. config/hooks.json The hook definitions. -template lets each hook read WEBHOOK_SECRET with getenv. config/sites.json Maps a site name to repo (GitHub owner/name), web_dir and branch (default main). scripts/pull-site.sh pull-site.sh <site-name>: clones or updates one site from sites.json. It exits with status 1 when the name is missing or unknown, or sites.json is absent. caddy-snippet.txt The Caddy site block for dbtools.greatwhitelab.net. hooks.json and sites.json also define a blog site (kirsch33/blog, served from /web/blog) that uses the same script. Requirements Docker with Compose, and a Caddy container on the external Docker network caddy_default. The image needs bash, git and jq, because pull-site.sh uses all three. The base image has only the webhook binary and /bin/sh; the Dockerfile adds them with apk. The host directory /web must be writable by the UID:GID in the user field of docker-compose.yml (1001:1001). Set it to the server user that owns the bind mounts. The site repository must be readable over anonymous HTTPS, because pull-site.sh clones https://github.com/<repo>.git without credentials. The GitHub webhook and webhook.env must use the same secret. Setup Copy webhook.env.example to webhook.env and set WEBHOOK_SECRET, for example from openssl rand -hex 32. Check and start the service: docker compose config --quiet docker compose up -d --build Add the block from caddy-snippet.txt to the Caddyfile and reload Caddy. On kirsch33/dbtools-wiki, add a webhook for push events with the payload URL https://dbtools.greatwhitelab.net/hooks/dbtools-wiki, the content type application/json and the same secret. -hotreload makes the webhook reload hooks.json when the file changes. A change to the Dockerfile needs docker compose up -d --build. To move to another base image, resolve its digest and rebuild on the wiki host.

developer-guide/developing/feature-warni.title: Feature Warnings | DB Tools
developer-guide/developing/feature-warni.summary: Feature Warnings A feature warning reports an actionable configuration or prerequisite problem. Active warnings block the commands named by their definitions and publish ribbon enablement updates. Warning state lasts for the current runtime session. It is not persisted to settings. The Settings window displays warning cards. The Settings button shows a warning icon, and the DB Tools tab receives a highlight when warnings exist. Command preflight and contextual edit flows use the same registered warning policy as ribbon controls. Defining warnings in manifest.yml Declare warnings under a settings pack: tool: settingsPacks: - key: structural.foundation_tags title: "Combined Foundation Tags" warnings: - id: core.structural.combined_tags title: "Combined Foundation Tags Disabled" message: "Use Settings -> Combined Foundation Tags -> Fix (Install/Repair) to repair prerequisites. Clear the warning afterward." disableTools: - DBTools.UpdateCombinedFoundationTags - DBTools.MoveCombinedFoundationTags - DBTools.OrganizeFoundationTypes Property Requirement and meaning id Required globally unique warning identity. title Required warning-card title. message Required description and corrective action. disableTools Optional list of registered ribbon internalName values. Use stable IDs such as core.library.invalid, core.structural.elevation_tags, and core.structural.joist_girder. List only commands that depend on the prerequisite. Name the problem, the affected operation, and the correction in the warning message. ToolWarningManifest carries the ID, title, message, and disabled-tool list. The manifest is metadata. It does not activate the warning by itself. Registering warning definitions Register a warning as the Warning member of SettingsPackRegistration<TOptions,TContext> in ToolModule.RegisterSettingsPacks. Settings Packs contains the full registration, including the required typed SettingsSection. Warning = new SettingsPackWarningRegistration<SettingsPackContext> { Id = warning.Id, Title = warning.Title, Message = warning.Message, ToolInternalNamesToDisable = warning.DisableTools, FlagGetter = context => context.HasWarning, FlagSetter = (context, active) => context.HasWarning = active } SettingsPackWarningRegistration<TContext> exposes these members: Member Type Required Id, Title, Message string Yes ToolInternalNamesToDisable IReadOnlyCollection<string>? No FlagGetter Func<TContext, bool> Yes FlagSetter Action<TContext, bool> Yes The registration extension validates required values at runtime. The bound runtime warning retains the exact context created by its pack. Callers cannot supply another context to its getter or setter. The context owns HasWarning for presentation and editing. The settings DTO owns persisted preferences such as AutoUpdateEnabled. IAutoUpdateSettings requires only that preference. Do not serialize a warning flag or derive command blocking from a saved flag. Triggering warnings Tools use DBTools.Core.Settings.Warnings.ISettingsWarningService: IReadOnlyCollection<ISettingsWarningDefinition> Definitions { get; } bool IsWarningActive(string warningId); SettingsWarningStateChange SetWarning(string warningId, bool active); warnings.SetWarning("core.structural.combined_tags", true); if (warnings.IsWarningActive("core.structural.combined_tags")) return; Blank or unknown IDs fail. Definitions must exist in the validated settings catalog before a tool uses them. Warning lookup is ordinal and case-sensitive. SetWarning updates session state and publishes the warning and aggregate visual state. SettingsWarningStateChange reports the prior and current state. The concrete SettingsWarningService owns active-ID enumeration and replay. SettingsWarningPublicationPolicy publishes individual warning changes, full replay, and aggregate HasWarnings. Tools receive the narrowed public interface, not internal publication operations. Validation and activation A warning-aware editor implements ISettingsWarningContext.WarningId and returns an invalid SettingsValidationResult for a configuration problem. The ID must belong to that pack. Use the actual result API: public Task<SettingsValidationResult> ValidateAsync(CancellationToken ct = default) { ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested(); return Task.FromResult(string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(LibraryPath) ? SettingsValidationResult.FromErrors("Select a library path.") : SettingsValidationResult.Success); } This excerpt checks an editor-owned LibraryPath. A real library validator must also check its required file/directory conditions. Conditional features can return Success when disabled if their configuration is unnecessary then. Do not report an unexpected I/O or programming exception as invalid settings. Validation has distinct publication rules: Operation Warning behavior Startup Load saved options into fresh runtimes without views. Activate invalid warning-aware packs. Do not proactively clear warnings. Open Settings Validate loaded options and publish warning state. Validate button Evaluate unsaved drafts and editor flags. Do not change shared command blocking. Save before commit Evaluate drafts and reject blocking invalid values. Do not publish draft decisions. Save after commit Validate saved values in fresh runtimes, project decisions, and replay published state. Reset Commit defaults, apply them, validate, and publish. ISettingsPackSaveValidation.BlockSaveOnInvalid determines whether an invalid draft blocks Save. Invalid settings and a validation exception are different outcomes. Startup logs a validation exception without activating its feature warning. Settings-window failures propagate through the normal error path. Startup disposes every runtime it creates. It retries a failed disposal once, logs persistent failures with the pack identity, and preserves cancellation when cleanup also fails. The warning evaluator uses the same validated SettingsCatalog as the Settings window. Auto-update task integration ViewActivationTask<TSettings> reads the current settings once during admission. It returns no admission when AutoUpdateEnabled is false or any configured warning is active. Otherwise it evaluates the tool predicate and returns an admission that captures that settings snapshot. The hook distinguishes two failures: An admission failure records a document-session failure and activates WarningIdsToSetOnFailure. A settings-read failure occurs at this boundary. A failure while executing an admitted operation shows the canonical auto-update failure banner and suppresses further runs for that document session. It does not activate feature warnings automatically. Tool-owned prerequisite checks can activate a warning explicitly, for example when required shared parameters are missing. Unexpected runtime exceptions must propagate to the hook's safe-execution boundary. See Hooks for admission, document-session identity, and failure handling. An active warning can disable the editor's toggle through ToggleEnabled. Changing the persisted AutoUpdateEnabled preference is a separate tool policy. It is not a required side effect of SetWarning. Warning UI and command blocking SettingsWarningViewModel wraps an ISettingsPackRuntimeWarning. It exposes WarningId, Title, Message, IsActive, Clear and Fix commands, and Fix availability. The warning card binds to that row state. Publication reaches ribbon controls in this order: The warning service publishes a WarningChangedEventArgs. RibbonSettingsObserver receives the published change. RibbonVisualUpdater applies its per-command enabled state. RibbonCompositionState updates registered buttons. RibbonComposer registers controls before subscribing to settings changes. RibbonVisualUpdater also applies aggregate Settings-icon and tab-highlight updates. RibbonSettingsObserver owns subscription lifetime and dispatcher delivery. RibbonCompositionState owns the registered controls and panel state. Command preflight checks every applicable active warning. Ribbon enablement instead applies each warning's latest update directly. If several warnings name one command, clearing one can visually enable its button while another still blocks execution. Give each disabled command one warning definition when its ribbon state must match command preflight. WarningChangedEventArgs carries WarningId, PackKey, IsActive, and ToolInternalNamesToDisable. WarningSetChangedEventArgs carries aggregate HasWarnings. Treat these as published state, not persistence requests. Clearing and fixing warnings Clear sets the bound context warning false and calls ISettingsWarningService.SetWarning(id, false). It does not repair prerequisites or save settings. A later validation or prerequisite check can activate the warning again. A tool can clear a warning programmatically after its prerequisite check succeeds: warnings.SetWarning("core.structural.combined_tags", false); Changing only a context property does not publish command availability. Use the service or the Settings validation workflow to synchronize published state. A context that implements IWarningFixProvider can add a Fix action: string FixWarningId { get; } string FixLabel { get; } Task FixWarningAsync(CancellationToken ct = default); The provider's warning ID must match the card. Blank IDs or labels fail construction. SettingsWarningViewModel invokes the provider, updates command state when the context changes, and logs action failures. Its ActionFailed event passes failures to Settings feedback. Disposal unsubscribes the context observer. Combined Foundation Tags uses Fix for Install/Repair and explicit refresh for shared parameter checks. Its constructor only prepares editor state. See Settings Packs for host context and persistence ordering. Examples Combined Combined Foundation Tags uses core.structural.combined_tags for Update Combined Foundation Tags, Move Combined Tags, and Organize Foundation Types. Transfer Drafting Views (TDV) uses core.library.invalid for Import From Library and Export To Library. Joist Girder Weights uses core.structural.joist_girder for its update command. Their manifests under src/Tools/ define the IDs and messages. See Testing Tools for warning-service test procedures.

developer-guide/developing/hooks.html.title: Hooks | DB Tools
developer-guide/developing/hooks.html.summary: Hooks Hooks attach tool behavior to Revit application events. Core's HookHost resolves registered implementations, owns the shared ViewActivated subscription, and coordinates initialization, rollback, and shutdown. Tool-owned lifecycle hooks manage subscriptions that need their own event adapters. Use IViewActivationTask for work triggered by a view change. Use IHookLifecycle for owned subscriptions such as contextual ribbon UI or dialog suppression. Register services through the tool module. Do not attach another copy of Core's ViewActivated handler. Hook architecture flowchart LR Revit[Revit events] --> Host[HookHost] Registry[ToolRegistry and DI] --> Host Host --> View[ViewActivationHook] Host --> Lifecycle[IHookLifecycle implementations] View --> Tasks[IViewActivationTask services] AppHooksToolModule registers the single ViewActivationHook service and its RegisterHook<ViewActivationHook, ViewActivationHook>() mapping. The hook collects IEnumerable<IViewActivationTask> from DI. ViewActivationHookDispatcher owns the outer safe-execution boundary. ViewActivationTaskRunner evaluates admissions and executes admitted tasks. HookCatalog accepts only ViewActivationHook and IHookLifecycle contracts. It resolves each registered implementation from the service provider and fails when a service is missing or does not implement its declared contract. New contracts require explicit catalog and host subscription support. Hooks run in response to Revit UI callbacks. Returning Task does not move API work to a background thread. Use asynchronous I/O where appropriate, avoid blocking the UI, and reacquire a valid Revit call gate before API work after an await. Modularity describes the synchronous callback restriction. Registering hooks Register both the concrete service and its hook mapping: public override void RegisterServices(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { services.AddSingleton<ContextualEditHook>(); } public override void RegisterHooks(ToolRegistry registry, ToolManifest manifest) { registry.RegisterHook<IHookLifecycle, ContextualEditHook>(); } This excerpt assumes a tool-owned ContextualEditHook : IHookLifecycle whose constructor dependencies are registered. Manifest and module setup is described in Creating New Tools. View-activation tasks use a factory registration. The Elevation Tags task needs manifest warning IDs in addition to its registered service dependencies: var warning = manifest.GetSingleSettingsPack().GetSingleWarning(manifest.Id); var warningIds = new[] { warning.Id }; services.AddSingleton<ElevationTagsUpdater>(); services.AddSingleton<IViewActivationTask>(sp => new ViewActivatedTask( sp.GetRequiredService<ISettingsProvider>(), sp.GetRequiredService<SettingsSection<ElevationTagsSettings>>(), sp.GetRequiredService<ISettingsWarningService>(), sp.GetRequiredService<ElevationTagsUpdater>(), sp.GetRequiredService<IErrorNotifier>(), sp.GetRequiredService<ILogger<ViewActivatedTask>>(), warningIds)); This excerpt follows Elevation Tags' App/Composition/ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs. The IReadOnlyCollection<string> warningIds constructor argument comes from the manifest, not automatic DI resolution. Every task must have a nonblank unique TaskId. All entries in WarningIdsToSetOnFailure must match registered warning definitions. The task registry validates these identities at construction. The IViewActivationTask System The public contract separates admission from execution: public interface IViewActivationTask { string TaskId { get; } string DisplayName { get; } IReadOnlyCollection<string> WarningIdsToSetOnFailure { get; } Task<ViewActivationAdmission?> AdmitAsync( UIApplication uiapp, ViewActivatedEventArgs args, CancellationToken ct); } AdmitAsync returns null to skip the attempt. A non-null ViewActivationAdmission captures the state that attempt will use: new ViewActivationAdmission(executionCt => ExecuteAsync(snapshot, executionCt)); The hook invokes the returned admission callback once for that attempt. Create a new admission for each event so it captures that event's state. ViewActivationTask Derive from ViewActivationTask<TSettings> for an auto-update task with typed settings. TSettings must implement IAutoUpdateSettings and have a public parameterless constructor. Its base constructor receives: ViewActivationTask( ISettingsProvider settingsProvider, SettingsSection<TSettings> settingsSection, ISettingsWarningService warnings, IErrorNotifier notifier, ILogger logger, string taskId, string displayName, IReadOnlyCollection<string> warningIds); The base admission sequence is: Check cancellation and read the current typed settings. Skip when AutoUpdateEnabled is false. Skip when any configured warning is active. Call the optional ShouldRunInternalAsync predicate. Capture that settings snapshot in an admission calling ExecuteInternalAsync. Override these methods with the exact signatures: protected override Task<bool> ShouldRunInternalAsync( UIApplication uiapp, ViewActivatedEventArgs args, MyToolSettings settings, CancellationToken ct) { var view = args.CurrentActiveView; return Task.FromResult(view != null && (view.ViewType == ViewType.FloorPlan || view.ViewType == ViewType.CeilingPlan)); } protected override Task ExecuteInternalAsync( UIApplication uiapp, ViewActivatedEventArgs args, MyToolSettings settings, CancellationToken ct) { return _updater.UpdateAsync(uiapp, args.CurrentActiveView, settings, ct); } This excerpt assumes a tool-owned updater with that operation. Inject its real implementation. Filter cheap conditions before expensive work. Use shared transaction services for modifications and synchronous callbacks inside them. Do not create a transaction around asynchronous work. The base exposes Logger and a protected banner helper. It reads no settings again during execution, so the admitted values remain consistent and settings-read failures occur at admission. Dispatch and failure policy The hook resolves the document from args.CurrentActiveView and returns when there is no active document/view. It visits tasks in DI registration order. Each task is evaluated and executed through the safe executor. Outcome Result Null admission Skip the task for this event. Admission failure Record a document-session failure and activate the task's warning IDs. Execution failure Show the canonical auto-update failure banner and record a document-session failure. Do not automatically activate feature warnings. Cancellation Preserve the canceled outcome rather than classify it as a runtime failure. A runtime failure suppresses subsequent attempts for the task/document session. The gate uses DocumentSessionKey. Save As or the first save can create a new key, and reopening a document starts a new session. Clearing a feature warning alone does not erase the recorded runtime failure for that key. Tool prerequisite checks may explicitly activate an actionable warning and return without executing the update. Unexpected updater exceptions propagate. Feature Warnings owns the distinction between invalid configuration, admission failure, and execution failure. Core suppresses routine logs and presentation on the outer event dispatch. Admission uses error-only banners without start/completion logs. An admitted execution logs start/completion, suppresses generic executor banners, and uses one canonical runtime-failure banner. Keep detailed probes at Trace and log meaningful state changes. Do not suppress failure logs unless another published lifecycle owner observes and records that exact failure. IHookLifecycle Lifecycle hooks implement three operations: public interface IHookLifecycle { Task InitializeAsync(UIControlledApplication application, CancellationToken ct); Task RollbackAsync(UIControlledApplication application, CancellationToken ct); void Shutdown(UIControlledApplication application); } InitializeAsync acquires subscriptions and other owned state. If initialization fails partway, the implementation must undo its own partial work and preserve both initialization and cleanup failures. Record ownership immediately after subscription, before later logging or callbacks can fail. RollbackAsync reverses attachment when later startup work fails. It can queue into a valid Revit context because its continuation may run outside the original UI callback. Shutdown runs synchronously in Revit's shutdown callback. It must finish owned unsubscribe/removal work before returning. It has no cancellation token and cannot publish background work for later completion. Host ordering and rollback HookHost.AttachAsync resolves handlers, initializes lifecycle actions in registration order, then force-queues its ViewActivated subscription. It publishes attached state only after all actions succeed. The host records each attempted owner before initialization begins. Successfully initialized actions roll back in reverse order if attachment fails. The failing initializer owns its partial cleanup. Normal shutdown also reaches attempted owners whose initialization or rollback is incomplete. HookAttachAction cancels pending attachment, prevents later initialization or rollback dispatch after shutdown is requested, and makes completed shutdown idempotent. Cancellation failure does not prevent its shutdown callback. A failed callback remains available for retry. Late asynchronous attachment completion cannot invoke Revit shutdown callbacks from a background thread. HookLifecycleCoordinator attempts every reverse-order teardown action and aggregates contextual failures. Hooks and view tasks follow registration order. Group dependent operations in one hook or task when their ordering is part of the behavior. Contextual ribbon injectors DBTools.Core.Tools.Hooks.ContextualRibbon.ContextualRibbonInjector implements IHookLifecycle and IDisposable. Derive from it for tool-specific Edit buttons on contextual tabs. Super Girt Tool (SGT) supplies ContextualEditHook as an example. The derived type supplies tool/button/event names, the registered contextual command type, target tabs, selection evaluation, button construction, and edit flow. The base owns selection-change observation, injected controls, system-ID state, safe execution, and the edit ExternalEvent. Initialization queues API work to create the edit event, subscribe to selection changes, and evaluate the initial state. A partial failure immediately attempts unsubscribe, contextual UI removal, and edit-event disposal. Rollback uses the queued cleanup path. Normal shutdown uses synchronous cleanup and the exact detach action captured at successful subscription. Create ExternalEvent objects only in valid Revit API contexts. Autodesk ribbon command callbacks are not such a context. The base creates/refreshes its edit event through its managed Revit entry path. Contextual edit validates ContextualEditCommandType through CommandPreflight, sharing normal command registration and warning policy. Do not duplicate the base's event subscription or button registry in a derived type. FindTargetTabs, EvaluateSelection, BuildButton, and RunEditFlow are the tool-specific extension points. Synchronous shutdown Revit's IExternalApplication.OnShutdown is synchronous. AppShutdownLifecycle.Shutdown invokes AppShutdownWorkflow.RunSynchronously in that callback. It cancels startup, detaches hooks, and disposes runtime hosts before returning. It disposes the startup cancellation source only when startup is complete or absent. It neither queues Revit work nor pumps the dispatcher. Unfinished startup or deferred observation yields Result.Failed after owned teardown attempts. Core tracks WPF DispatcherOperation handles. Posting records ownership before BeginInvoke and rechecks retirement after the handle arrives. DispatcherOperationRegistry.Retire closes posting, releases callbacks and cancellation registrations, and aborts pending operations without executing their payloads. Their completion Tasks remain pending. Posts refused before queueing return canceled Tasks. WindowStaticRuntime.Reset does not retire that queue. Logger, ribbon, notification, and progress posts use WpfDispatcher.Post. Callback faults remain observable. A fault in an error reporter stays on the completion Task rather than escaping into Dispatcher.UnhandledException. Shutdown must not pump WPF or await retired dispatcher work. Extending and debugging hooks Use IHookLifecycle for another owned application subscription. Add an event-specific contract only when its dispatch shape requires one. Such a change must update the catalog, resolution, subscription, safe-execution policy, rollback, synchronous detach, and tests together. HookHost rejects an unknown contract. Registering it alone cannot attach an event. Symptom Check Lifecycle hook never initializes Register both its concrete DI service and RegisterHook<IHookLifecycle,T>() mapping. View task never runs Check its IViewActivationTask registration, settings, active warnings, predicate, and document-session failure gate. Startup rejects the task Check nonblank unique task IDs and known warning IDs. Handler resolution fails Register the concrete type and its constructor dependencies. UI freezes Remove synchronous waits and long work from UI callbacks. Re-enter the gate for API work after an await. Cleanup fails Inspect contextual errors for each unsubscribe, UI removal, and disposal attempt. Inspect %APPDATA%/DBTools/Logs/ first. Use the Settings Debug Mode control for runtime diagnostics rather than adding an unrelated logging configuration. See Testing Tools for fixture placement, compilation, and execution commands.

developer-guide/developing/modularity.ht.title: Modularity | DB Tools
developer-guide/developing/modularity.ht.summary: Modularity Tools use Core for execution, transactions, settings, logging, and window lifecycle. Presentation owns stable WPF shells, controls, resources, and themes. Tool assemblies own feature behavior, raw views, and ViewModels. Use constructor injection inside services. Resolve the first workflow from ICommandContext at the command boundary. Creating New Tools describes assembly ownership and module registration. Service lifetimes The application service root lasts for one runtime generation. A command or modeless session owns a run scope for Revit-dependent services. Service Lifetime Purpose ISafeExecutor Singleton Error policy, logging, and notifications at entrypoints. IAlertService Singleton Alert and selection dialogs. ISettingsProvider Singleton Fresh typed reads and atomic batch commits. ToolRegistry Application runtime Command and hook registrations. IRevitRunScope Scoped Current Revit application and document access. IRevitCallGate Scoped Synchronous API callbacks in a valid Revit context. ITransactionRunner Scoped Transactions for model changes. ITransactionGroupService Scoped Group health and commit/rollback. Use ILogger<T> through injection and context.Logger at command boundaries. The application logging host owns logger lifetime. Keep Document, UIDocument, and run-scope references within their command or session lifetime. Pass operation-specific document inputs or obtain verified current state from the run scope. Dispose the command/session scope only after its owned work and cleanup finish. Safe execution DBTools.Core.SafeExecution.Domain.ISafeExecutor defines two boundaries: Task RunAsync( Func<Task> action, ILogger logger, IErrorNotifier? notifier, SafeExecutionOptions opts, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<SafeExecutionResult> RunWithoutThrowingAsync( Func<Task> action, ILogger logger, IErrorNotifier? notifier, SafeExecutionOptions opts, CancellationToken ct = default); RunAsync propagates failures. RunWithoutThrowingAsync records an explicit outcome for a caller that must contain failure, such as a Revit event callback. Both provide correlation IDs, timing, cancellation admission, exception logging, and configured notifications. ToolCommand already owns this boundary. Let workflow failures reach it. SafeExecutionOptions requires an operation name: var options = new SafeExecutionOptions("Inspect Model") { BannerMode = SafeExecutionOptions.Mode.ErrorOnly }; await executor.RunAsync(InspectAsync, logger, notifier, options, ct); Option Default Effect LogStart true Log entry. LogCompletion true Log completion. LogFailure true Log a failed operation. BannerMode SuccessAndError Show success/error banners, errors only, or neither. FailureSurface Surface Surface fatal errors through the configured failure surface. CorrelationId Unspecified Supply an existing execution correlation ID. ErrorBanner(name, logStart, logCompletion) selects error-only banners. SuppressFailurePresentation(name) suppresses banners, fatal presentation, and routine start/completion logs while retaining failure logging. Disable LogFailure only when an already-published lifecycle owner observes and logs that same fault. Preserve the failed Task. App composition adapts the UI-owned log surface to ISafeExecutionFailureSurface. Window error boundaries use IWindowErrorLogSurface and WindowErrorPresenter. Consumers depend on these contracts rather than constructing concrete logger or notification windows. Use structured log fields: logger.LogInformation("Processing {Count} elements in {Document}", count, document.Title); logger.LogError(exception, "Inspection failed for {Document}", document.Title); Use IAlertService for user decisions and IErrorNotifier for banners. Propagate failures through the safe-execution boundary with their context. Revit run scopes and call gates IRevitRunScope exposes UIApplication, CallGate, GetActiveUiDocument(), GetActiveDocument(), and GetVerifiedActiveDocument(expectedDocument, context). The verification method checks validity and DocumentSessionKey equality before returning the active document. Use the verification method before operating on a retained document. Run profile Gate Use InlineUi InlineRevitCallGate Commands already executing in a valid Revit API callback. QueuedModeless QueuedRevitCallGate Modeless work through the App-owned ExternalEvent host. The gate accepts synchronous callbacks: Task RunAsync(Action<UIApplication> work, CancellationToken ct = default, RevitCallGateMode mode = RevitCallGateMode.Auto); Task<T> RunAsync<T>(Func<UIApplication, T> work, CancellationToken ct = default, RevitCallGateMode mode = RevitCallGateMode.Auto); Await the returned Task outside the callback. Do not pass async lambdas into the gate. Async-state-machine Actions and known Task/ValueTask result shapes are rejected before execution. An awaitable hidden in object or an interface is rejected after the callback runs. Side effects remain. Custom awaiters are outside this check. A Revit API callback's context applies to its synchronous prefix. An async continuation must acquire a valid gate again before using the Revit API. InGate reports execution within a gate callback. It does not make arbitrary background work safe. On normal host retirement, pending queued work is dropped and its Tasks remain pending, even if cancellation arrives later. Shutdown must not await these Tasks. Failed-startup cleanup cancels pending work instead. See Revit execution for the full callback and shutdown contract. Transactions ITransactionRunner wraps synchronous model modifications: Task RunInActiveDocumentAsync(string name, Action<RevitTransactionContext> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<T> RunInActiveDocumentAsync<T>(string name, Func<RevitTransactionContext, T> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task RunInDocumentAsync(Document doc, string name, Action<RevitTransactionContext> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<T> RunInDocumentAsync<T>(Document doc, string name, Func<RevitTransactionContext, T> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Use transaction.Document inside the callback: await transactions.RunInDocumentAsync(document, "DB Tools - Set Mark", transaction => { var element = transaction.Document.GetElement(elementId); element.LookupParameter("Mark").Set(mark); }, ct); The runner selects a SubTransaction when the document is modifiable and a new Transaction otherwise. It enforces document context and applies TransactionFailurePreprocessor. The callback rules match the call gate: no async Actions or Task/ValueTask results. Give each transaction a descriptive undo name. Transaction groups ITransactionGroupService groups several transactions into one undo operation: bool IsActive { get; } Task BeginAsync(string name, CancellationToken ct = default); Task FinalizeAsync(TransactionGroupFinalization finalization, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<bool> IsGroupHealthyAsync(CancellationToken ct = default); Finalize with TransactionGroupFinalization.Commit to assimilate the group or Rollback to discard it. IsGroupHealthyAsync returns true when no group exists and false when an active group has lost its healthy started state. The session/workflow owner must finalize on success, failure, and cancellation. Use a separate cancellation token for cleanup when the operation is canceled. Attempt all owned cleanup and retain both the operation and finalization errors. Do not use an unguarded finally exception that hides the operation's failure. Long-lived tool sessions also own the ordering of persistence, window closure, group finalization, and scope disposal. Alerts and selection IAlertService exposes request-based dialogs: AlertResult Show(AlertRequest request); bool Confirm(string message, IWindowOwnerHandleProvider ownerHandleProvider, string title = "DB Tools"); T? SelectSingle<T>(AlertSelectionRequest<T> request) where T : class; IReadOnlyList<T> SelectMultiple<T>(AlertSelectionRequest<T> request) where T : class; Confirmation requires an owner provider. In a command: var alerts = context.Resolve<IAlertService>(); if (!alerts.Confirm("Delete the selected elements?", context.OwnerHandleProvider)) return; Selection requests supply choices, a display function, window title, header, and owned window options. For example: var selected = alerts.SelectSingle(new AlertSelectionRequest<Level>( levels, level => level.Name, "Select Level", "Target Level", new AlertWindowOptions(context.OwnerHandleProvider)) { Message = "Choose the target level." }); Core owns selection policy, body construction, and typed result extraction. Settings Inject ISettingsProvider and the typed SettingsSection<T>. Call Get(section) at the operation boundary for a fresh snapshot. Reads layer appsettings.json and the current per-year user file. Commit one or more section writes as a batch: var options = settings.Get(section); options.AutoUpdateEnabled = true; await settings.CommitAsync(new[] { section.CreateWrite(options) }, ct); Do not retain a settings snapshot in a singleton when subsequent operations need saved changes. Settings Packs owns DTO restrictions, source-generated metadata, file locking, save timing, and post-commit errors. Shared UI resources DBTools.Presentation.ThemeBrushKeys exposes ComponentResourceKey values. Use dynamic resources so the window's theme supplies each brush: <Border xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation" xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml" xmlns:theme="clr-namespace:DBTools.Presentation;assembly=DBTools.Presentation" Background="{DynamicResource {x:Static theme:ThemeBrushKeys.Surface}}"> <TextBlock Text="Inspection" Foreground="{DynamicResource {x:Static theme:ThemeBrushKeys.Body}}" /> </Border> Keys cover brand, surface, text, status, and DataGrid brushes. Use the actual members in ThemeBrushKeys.cs and tokens in Resources/Tokens.xaml. Do not invent string keys or duplicate color values. Window-scoped resources avoid changing another add-in's theme. See the Theme System. Merge the stable Presentation theme into a raw view through ResourceUri: <Grid xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation" xmlns:resources="clr-namespace:DBTools.Presentation.Resources;assembly=DBTools.Presentation"> <Grid.Resources> <ResourceDictionary> <ResourceDictionary.MergedDictionaries> <ResourceDictionary Source="{resources:ResourceUri Resources/Theme.xaml}" /> </ResourceDictionary.MergedDictionaries> </ResourceDictionary> </Grid.Resources> </Grid> ResourceUri selects the loaded Presentation assembly's versioned resource URI. Keep raw views on stable resources rather than constructing payload pack URIs. Design tokens Resources/Tokens.xaml defines spacing, padding, corner radius, and typography. Use the token with the property type it expects: Token Type and value Spacing4, Spacing8, Spacing16 Thickness values of 4, 8, and 16. Spacing4.Value, Spacing8.Value, Spacing16.Value Double values for scalar properties. Pad8, Card.Padding Thickness values of 8 and 16,12. Radius4, Radius8 CornerRadius values of 4 and 8. FontSize.Body, FontSize.Title, FontSize.Header Double values of 13, 16, and 20. Tool-window sessions A raw tool view uses framework or stable Presentation types. It has no Window root, x:Class, code-behind event attributes, tool CLR namespaces, payload BAML, or implicit templates for tool types. Bind display values explicitly. Core's ToolWindowFactory installs the theme, owner, icon, error boundary, and progress lifecycle before parsing. It registers the session for normal closure and runtime-generation retirement: using var xaml = new MemoryStream(ToolWindowXaml.ReadEmbeddedResource( typeof(MyToolWindowViewModel).Assembly, "DBTools.ToolViews.MyTool.MyToolWindow.xaml")); var session = factory.Create(ToolWindowKind.Modal, xaml, viewModel, new ToolWindowOptions { Title = "My Tool", Width = 800, Height = 600 }); _ = session.ShowDialog(); Use ToolWindowKind.Modeless and session.Show() for a modeless surface. Register payload handlers and owned cleanup through the session. A custom initializeShell callback owns the initializer it creates and must register its disposal through session.AddCleanup. Normal close dispatches payload Closed handlers before releasing owned state. Retirement of an open session also clears its view graph. Keep the application run scope alive through failure-bearing session completion. Window.Close() alone does not establish that asynchronous cleanup finished. Presentation owns shells and ToolWindowCallbackScope. Core and tool assemblies can belong to a replaceable product generation. Stable controls and resources must not retain a retired ViewModel, callback, or tool type. This contract also applies to Settings, alerts, logger windows, banners, and progress UI. Sandbox Integration covers previews and native WPF validation. Hooks covers subscriptions that also need generation-safe shutdown.

developer-guide/developing/new-tool-guid.title: Creating New Tools | DB Tools
developer-guide/developing/new-tool-guid.summary: Creating New Tools A DB Tools tool owns its source, manifest, resources, production assembly, and tests. App discovers embedded manifests, registers services, and composes ribbon controls. Each tool assembly ships under the product year's Tools/ directory. Service and settings modules follow the same assembly contract as ribbon tools. Use this page to create the tool boundary.
